item.title: Living in Gurro and working in Ticino as a border worker
item.description: Move to Gurro and commute to the Canton of Ticino: distances, crossings, tax regime Permit G, costs and practical scenarios.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Gurro is a small Italian town in Val Cannobina, far from the great Ticino crossings - The frontier tax regime applies in Switzerland, with tax credit in Italy - New Agreement in force from 1 January 2024: €10,000 deductible for new frontier workers - Low real estate costs compared to Ticino, but long travel times
## Key facts - **What**: Transfer to Gurro with commuting to the Canton of Ticino under Permit G - When: Regime active from 1 January 2024 (New Agreement signed on 23 December 2020) - Where: Val Cannobina (VB), Italian-Swiss border Verbano-Cusio-Ossola / Ticino area - Who: Border employee, AFC/ESTV (federal tax), Ticino cantonal authorities, INPS - Amount: Tax at source only in CH; tax credit in Italy (EC framework of 730) - Amount: Old frontier workers exemption €7,500 (transitory 2024–2033), new €10,000 deductible
Gurro is a village of a few hundred inhabitants nestled in Val Cannobina, in the province of Verbano-Cusio-Ossola. Those considering moving here to work as a border worker in Canton Ticino must start from a physical fact: distance. The municipality is decentralised with respect to the large crossings of the Como-Varese-Lugano axis, and the route to the Ticino work areas necessarily passes through valley roads with long travel times. The choice is not only logistical, it is also fiscal: for employees with G Permit, ## In brief - Swiss AVS/LPP/LAMal costs affect net pay - Commute times Gurro-Ticino: estimated scenario, not verified by source - Italian cost of living significantly lower than in Ticino - Choose areas with stable internet coverage for hybrid remote work
## Key facts - **What**: Cross-border payslip: AVS/AI/IPG, AD, LAINF, LPP deductions - When: Regime in force since 2024 - Where: Canton Ticino — employers based in CH - Who: Employee with G Permit, SUVA for accidents, Swiss pension funds - Amount: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee; AD/AC 1.1% (cap CHF 148,200)
Before signing a rental contract in Gurro, it is worth simulating the net pay. The Swiss gross salary is subject to mandatory deductions that have no direct equivalents in Italy: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% borne by the employee, unemployment insurance (AD/AC) at 1.1% up to the cap of CHF 148,200, LAINF premiums (occupational and non-occupational accidents) between 0.7% and 1.5%, and LPP contributions (occupational pension) ranging from 7% to 18% depending on the age bracket, starting from age 25. On top of these come cantonal and municipal source tax. The move from gross to net can hold surprises: to avoid unpleasant ones it is useful to use the [cross-border salary calculator](nav:calculator) before making relocation decisions.
### Fixed costs and cost of living The flip side is the cost of living. In Canton Ticino rental rates are noticeably higher than in Val Cannobina: a comparison scenario (data not specified by the source) indicates that renting a three-room apartment in a suburban Ticino area generally costs more than double compared to a comparable property in Gurro, where the market is niche and very limited. Health insurance also weighs heavily: G cross-border workers can exercise the LAMal opt-out right, choosing between Swiss health insurance and Italian coverage, with adult deductibles between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500 depending on the insurance model. The choice must be recalculated year by year based on the premium, the deductible, and the propensity to use healthcare facilities in CH or in Italy.
### Realistic commuting Those living in Gurro and wanting to reach Ticino work areas must consider that the valley floor is mainly connected via the SS 666 toward Malesco and then Cannobio, and onward to the border. Commute times (data not specified by the source) are subject to roadworks and weather, especially in winter. For more flexible professions, partial remote work is viable, drastically reducing commuting days. On the currency exchange front, the [CHF/EUR comparator](nav:exchange) helps understand what the Swiss net is really worth once converted into euros to pay household utilities.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## In brief - Operational steps: G Permit, LAMal registration, Italian tax code - Deadlines: Italian tax return even if taxed only in Switzerland - Site tools to simulate payslips and plan the move
## Key facts - **What**: Start-up checklist for a new cross-border resident in Gurro - When: Within the first 14 days of work in CH for the G Permit - Where: Municipality of Gurro (IT) + Canton Ticino (CH) - Who: SEM for the permit, AFC/ESTV for source tax, INPS for contribution position - Amount: Double taxation avoided through a tax credit (Quadro CE, 730)
### Step-by-step procedure First step: the Swiss employer initiates the procedure for the G Permit with the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration). The new hire receives the permit and can register with the registry office of their Italian municipality of residence, in this case Gurro. Second step: source tax is withheld directly by the employer according to the rates set by the Ticino cantonal tax authority, with remittance to the AFC/ESTV. The worker receives a monthly payslip showing the net amount already deducted. Third step: every year the cross-border worker is still required to file an Italian tax return (Form 730), indicating in Quadro CE the Swiss income and the tax credit to avoid double taxation.
### Decisions to make immediately Three choices must be made before the first salary. The first is health insurance: the LAMal right of option must be exercised within the first three months; the decision is binding and determines access to care in CH or IT. The second is pension provision: enrolment in the Swiss pension fund (LPP) is mandatory from the age of 25; the employer pays half of the contributions and the employee the other half. The third is the current account: to receive the salary, a CHF account with a Swiss bank is advisable, with periodic conversion to EUR via the [exchange rate comparator](nav:exchange) to reduce conversion costs.
### When it really makes sense The scenario in which moving to Gurro makes sense is when you have stable employment in Canton Ticino with a permanent contract and a salary that justifies absorbing commuting costs. If the job is precarious or low-paid, travel time quickly erodes the salary advantage. To assess the convenience, the first tool to use is the [tax calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator), which compares the Swiss net salary, Italian taxes and the real cost of living in Italy.
Fine-tune planning with the [net salary calculator](nav:payslip) and keep an eye on [border crossing wait times](nav:border) to organise departure times.

item.title: Living in Schignano and working in Ticino: a practical guide
item.description: Border from Schignano: tax legislation, AVS/LPP, permit G. What you need to know about taxes, contributions and administrative procedures.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Tax at source withheld only in Switzerland; no double taxation with Italian tax credit - From 1 January 2024: New active Agreement; deductible € 10,000 (new frontier workers) - AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7-18%, LAMal mandatory with option right - G-permit valid for 5 years, renewable by the cantonal authority Ticino
## Key facts - **What**: G Permit Frontier, Schignano-Ticino - When: From 1 January 2024 (New Agreement in force) - Where: Lombardy → Canton Ticino - Who: Employee, INPS + AVS - Tax: Withholding only in CH; IT personal income tax 23-43% (with credit for CH taxes) - CH contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7-18%, LAINF 0.7-1.5% - Permit: G (border), 5 years renewable
The border worker who lives in Schignano, Lombardy, and works in Ticino falls under the regime of cross-border workers regulated by the Italian-Swiss Convention of 9 December 1976 and the New Frontier Agreement (signed on 23 December 2020, in force from 1 January 2024). This status has tax, social security and organisational implications that differ significantly from the pure Italian employee or Swiss resident.
### Taxation of the Schignano-Ticino border crossing
Income tax at source is only withheld in Switzerland. The frontier worker does not pay double taxation: Italy avoids the double burden by resorting to the tax credit in the EC Framework form of the tax return (730). ### Social security contributions and compulsory insurance
The border crossing paid in Ticino adheres to the Swiss social security system. The AVS (old-age disability pension), AI (disability insurance) and IPG (loss of earnings allowance) are retained to the extent of 5.3% on the gross salary for the employee; the company pays the additional 5.3% on behalf of the worker. In addition there are unemployment insurance contributions (AD/AC) of 1.1%, limited to a ceiling of CHF 148,200 per annum, and accident insurance (LAINF) between 0.7 and 1.5%. To these is added occupational pension insurance (LPP), the second Swiss pillar, which represents a share between 7 and 18% of the gross salary depending on the age group (from 25 years). While AVS/AI/IPG are mandatory by law, the LPP is conditional on registration with the company's pension fund.
At the same time, the border worker remains registered with the Italian INPS for the payment of Italian social security contributions (about 9-10% of the declared income), with which he accumulates pension rights in the Italian system. This double contribution is lawful and does not generate conflict: each country recognizes the contribution paid in the other in the event of progress towards retirement.
### LAMal's choice: right of option and rewards
Health insurance (LAMal) in Switzerland is mandatory by law. Group G border workers have the right of option:
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure: How to become a Schignano–Ticino cross-border commuter
The administrative path involves three main steps. **First: G Permit application.** The cantonal Migration offices (SEM) or the cantonal police authority where the work will take place (Ticino) must be contacted. The application must be submitted jointly by the Swiss employer and the future employee. Required documents include: a valid passport or ID card, certificate of good conduct, employment contract, and documentation of the employer's registration with the Companies Register. The G Permit has long-term validity (generally 5 years, renewable) and allows daily commuting from the place of residence in Italy to the workplace in Ticino.
Second: simultaneous INPS registration. Once employed in Ticino, the worker must register with the Italian INPS as a salaried employee, reporting the expected gross Swiss income and the job category. This creates the Italian social security file alongside the Swiss AVS. The Swiss employer usually assists in transmitting social security data to the Italian authorities (CE coordination forms). Third: LAMal choice. Within the deadlines set by the employer (usually 3 months from hiring), the cross-border commuter declares whether to remain covered by the Italian CMI or to opt for a Swiss LAMal. The choice is not binding in perpetuity, but changing coverage requires notification to the employer and the relevant funds.
### Deadlines, checks, and useful tools
Before the transition from Schignano, it is advisable to check: the location of the workplace in Ticino (Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno), which determines the withholding tax rate and the competent canton for the permit; nationality and passport (the G Permit is issued to EU/EFTA citizens, with a simplified procedure); the Italian contribution history, to avoid gaps in INPS registration. Use the [cross-border salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the monthly net pay in CHF, taking into account Swiss tax deductions and the Italian tax credit. Consult the [G vs B Permit comparator](nav:permit-compare) to assess whether the B Permit (effective residence in Ticino) might be a preferable future choice. Check the [waiting times at border crossings](nav:border) (Brogeda, Chiasso, Mendrisio) to plan daily commuting in an informed way.

item.title: Living in Solbiate and working in Ticino as a border worker

## Key facts - **What**: New bilateral Italy-Switzerland agreement on border taxation - When: Effective January 1, 2024 (signed December 23, 2020) - Where: Frontier workers residing in Italy (province of Como), I work in Ticino - Who: New (after 17/7/2023) and old (before 17/7/2023) border guards - Deductible: €10,000 (new), €7,500 (old, transitional regime 2024-2033) - Taxation: Tax at source in Switzerland (5.3% AVS/AI/IPG); credit in Italy via 730 - Permit: Category G, 5 years, renewable
From 1 January 2024, the new border agreement between Italy and Switzerland has recalibrated the rights and duties of those who live in Solbiate with Cagno (province of Como) and work in Ticino. Signed on 23 December 2020 and operational since 2024, the agreement introduces a clear tax exemption and reduces the administrative complexity that characterised previous regimes.
There are two categories of border crossers. The “old frontier workers” — those who already had the status before July 17, 2023 — maintain an exemption of 7,500 euros per year from Italian income until December 31, 2033, after which they will switch to the standard regime. The "new frontier workers" (hired ### Why choose Solbiate with Cagno as a border resident
Solbiate con Cagno is located in the province of Como, a few kilometres from the border with the Canton of Ticino. This proximity is the first advantage: travel times to the main Ticino poles (Lugano, Mendrisio, Bellinzona) are limited, especially if the employer is located in the south (Lugano, Chiasso) or in intermediate areas. The cost of living in Solbiate is generally lower than in Ticino, both for accommodation (rentals and real estate purchases) and for daily services (food, utilities). Many border workers choose this area to live in well-organized Italian communities, with school, health and cultural services more in line with their habits, while maintaining the economic and social advantages of Swiss work.
The disadvantages are not negligible. Daily commuting to Ticino (passing through passes such as Brogeda, Chiasso or Gaggiolo) involves an expense for fuel and motorway (A2 from Como to the south), as well as the risk of queues during peak hours. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure: how to become a cross-border worker in Solbiate
Step 1. Make sure you have a job offer in Ticino. The G permit is granted only on a contractual basis. If you don't yet have a contract, use job search platforms specialized in Ticino offers or contact recruitment agencies that operate in the cross-border worker sector. Once you have received the offer and signed the contract with the Ticino employer, proceed with the permit application.
Step 2. Apply for the G permit with the competent Swiss authorities. The application is submitted through SECO (State Secretariat for the Economy) or via SEM (State Secretariat for Migration). Required documents include the signed employment contract, a valid identity document, proof of residence in Italy, and a criminal record certificate. The permit is valid for 5 years and the process typically takes 2-4 weeks.
Step 3. Register with INPS in Italy as a cross-border dependent worker. The application is submitted to the territorial branch of INPS in Como. You will need the employment contract, identity card, tax identification code, and proof of residence in Italy. INPS will coordinate with the Swiss system (AVS) to avoid duplicate contributions and ensure recognition of payments in both systems.
Step 4. Open a Swiss bank account to receive your salary in CHF. Many Swiss banks have simplified procedures for cross-border workers residing in the Como province. Some cross-border workers also maintain an Italian account to manage local expenses and exchange CHF-EUR according to personal needs.
Step 5. Choose health insurance. In the Swiss LAMal system, a G category cross-border worker has the right of choice (reinforced choice): they can remain in the Italian system or register with a Swiss health insurance fund. Adult deductibles in LAMal range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500. This is an important decision as it involves access to Ticino health services and monthly insurance premiums.
Step 6. Plan your annual tax return. Every year, in May, complete the 730 declaration at the Tax Agency in Como. In section CE, declare your Swiss income and tax credits for taxes paid to the AFC, applying the exemption (€10,000 if you are a new cross-border worker, €7,500 if you are an established cross-border worker under transitional regime). Always keep bank statements, withholding certificates from the AFC, and documentation on the Swiss AVS to avoid disputes.

item.title: Senna Comasco and border crossing work in Ticino: a practical guide
item.description: Senna Comasco is just a few kilometres from the Ponte Tresa crossing and Chiasso: connections, taxation and cost of living for border crossers.

## In a nutshell - Tax at source only in Switzerland, tax credit in Italy - New Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500, regime 2024–2033 - New frontier workers: deductible €10,000
## Key facts - **What**: Italian-Swiss border tax regime - When: New Agreement signed 23/12/2020, effective 1/1/2024 - Where: Canton Ticino (Switzerland) - Who: AFC/ESTV (federal), cantonal administrations, INPS, Revenue Agency - Amount: Old frontier exemption €7,500; new deductible €10,000 - Reference: Italy-Switzerland double taxation agreement of 9/12/1976 - IT ratification: Law 83 of 13/6/2023
Living in Senna Comasco and working in Ticino as a border worker is a concrete scenario for those looking for an Italian residence a few kilometres from the border. The municipality, located in the province of Como, enjoys a strategic position: it is a few kilometres from the Ponte Tresa and Chiasso/Brogeda crossings, two of the most used crossing points by Italian workers who enter the Canton of Ticino every morning.
From a legal point of view, the Italian worker residing in Senna Comasco who is hired by a Swiss employer falls into the category of border workers with a G permit. Switzerland is not a member of the European Union or the EEA, so the movement of people is regulated by specific bilateral agreements between Rome and Bern, and not by European free movement. The Canton of Ticino withholds the tax at source according to its own tables, published by the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV) at the federal level and then managed by the cantonal tax administrations. To these are added the Swiss compulsory social contributions, which the employer deducts from the paycheck of the border employee as for any other worker in Switzerland.
### Social deductions in Switzerland The following main items appear on the paycheck of a border worker with a G permit, all taken from the gross salary: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% paid by the employee, AD (unemployment insurance) at 1.1%, with an annual ceiling of CHF 148'200 on which the contribution is calculated; LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5% according to the branch of activity; LPP (compulsory occupational pension) with rates ranging from 7% to 18% depending on the age group, from 25 years. Before moving to Senna Comasco to work in Ticino, it is advisable to handle the bureaucratic steps in a precise order. The first step is signing the employment contract with the Swiss employer, who will submit the application for a G permit to the cantonal authorities. ### Step-by-step procedure to become a cross-border worker Here are the key steps, in chronological order:
**1. Obtain the G permit.** The Swiss employer submits the application to the cantonal migration office. The Municipality of Senna Comasco will subsequently issue the Italian certificate of residence required for the procedure.

item.title: Living in Binago and working in Ticino as a border worker
item.description: Binago, in the province of Como, is a few kilometres from the passes towards the Canton of Ticino: costs, taxation and commuting times for commuters.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Binago (CO) is a few km from the passes towards the Canton of Ticino - Tax at source in Switzerland, tax credit in Italy - New Agreement in force from 1 January 2024, ratifies Law 83/2023 - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500, transitional regime 2024–2033
## Key facts - **What**: Withholding tax withheld only in Switzerland - When: Double taxation agreement signed 9 December 1976 - Where: Canton Ticino, on the border with the province of Como - Who: AFC/ESTV (federal) + cantonal tax administrations - Old frontier exemption: €7,500 (before 17/7/2023) - Excess for new frontier workers: €10,000 - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% to be paid by the employee - New Agreement: in force from 1 January 2024
Binago is an Italian municipality in the province of Como located near the border with Switzerland. Its location makes it a natural starting point for workers who return daily to Italy after a shift in Ticino. However, those who evaluate the move from other Lombard municipalities to Binago must keep in mind a precise regulatory framework, because cross-border commuting is not a logistical choice: it is a tax and social security relationship between two States.
### The Italian-Swiss setting Income tax on employees of border workers is withheld ONLY in Switzerland, according to the rates established by federal and cantonal laws and administered by AFC/ESTV at the federal level and by the administrations ## Practical analysis
The decisive point for those who choose Binago as a residence is not only the kilometer distance from the Ticino workplace, but the combination of three factors: Italian real estate cost, Swiss source rate and management of the tax return. Let's see them one at a time.
### What changes for old and new frontiersmen Those who were already border workers before 17 July 2023 benefit from the €7,500 exemption and a transitional regime that expires in 2033: in fact, a band of income is not taxed in either Italy or Switzerland. On the other hand, new frontier workers, i.e. those who start working in Ticino after that date, have a deductible of €10,000. They are two separate regimes, both in force since 1 January 2024.
On the Swiss side, the Swiss payroll suffers the mandatory withholding taxes: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% borne by the employee, unemployment insurance (AD/AC) 1.1% within the maximum of CHF 148'200, LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the risk, and LPP (occupational pension) with rates ranging from 7% to 18% by age group, from 25 years.
### Italian personal income tax and tax credit The Italian IRPEF, referred to in the EC framework of 730, follows the standard steps: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000. This is not double taxation: taxes paid in Switzerland are recognised as a credit, preventing the same income from being taxed twice
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## What to do before moving to Binago
Moving as a cross-border worker is not just about buying a house: it means aligning three key areas (civil residence, work permit, and health coverage) within precise thresholds and deadlines. An operational checklist helps avoid the most common mistakes.
### Step-by-step procedure 1. **Permit verification**: the G permit (cross-border worker) is issued by the cantonal foreign police authority upon authorization from SEM (State Secretariat for Migration), not SECO. The Swiss employer submits the application to the competent cantonal service. 2. Civil registration: residence in Binago must be communicated to the Municipality within the legal deadlines, with a direct impact on the local health authority (ASL), pediatrician, and family doctors under agreement with Lombardy. 3. Payslip and contributions: ask the employer for details of AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF, and LPP deductions, and verify enrollment in the LPP pension fund from age 25. 4. LAMal: decide whether to exercise the option right for Swiss LAMal or maintain Italian coverage, comparing deductibles, premiums, and family member coverage. 5. Tax return: every year the cross-border worker files the 730 form in Italy, completing section CE for the tax credit on the source tax withheld in Switzerland.
### Recommended areas and connections Binago is connected to the Como road network, from which the border crossings towards Canton Ticino can be reached in reasonable times. For travel times to the crossings (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa), it is useful to regularly check traffic data: border queues can turn a short trip into a lengthy commitment.
### When it makes sense (and when it doesn't) Moving to Binago makes sense if you have a stable job in Ticino, accept daily commuting, and want to lower rent or property purchase prices compared to Swiss cross-border municipalities. It does not make sense if the employer applies remote work beyond the threshold allowed by the new agreement, because cross-border status requires physically returning to Italy.
To simulate the tax and contribution impact on your salary, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator). To compare the cost of living between Ticino and the Italian border area, go to the [cost of living comparator](nav:cost-of-living). For a complete checklist for your first day of work in Switzerland, see the [first day guide](nav:first-day).

1. The Ticino employer submits the work permit application to the competent cantonal office (Department of Education and Social Security of Canton Ticino). 2. After cantonal approval, the application is forwarded to the SEM for the issuance of the G permit. 3. Once the permit has been obtained, the frontier worker can start working regularly in Switzerland and must comply with the tax and contribution rules of the New Agreement.
The duration of the G permit is usually five years and requires periodic renewal. Throughout its validity period, the frontier worker is subject to the tax and contribution laws of the New Frontier Worker Agreement, with well-defined rights and obligations.
### Calculating net salary: which tools to use
Determining precisely the monthly net pay from a Ticino payslip is complex, as federal and cantonal rates, AVS/AI/LPP contributions, mandatory health insurance (LAMal), and Italian tax deductions all come into play. Use [the salary calculator](nav:calculator) on our site to simulate your monthly net pay based on your Swiss gross salary, age bracket, marital status, and family dependants. This tool takes mandatory contributions and the specific features of the New Agreement into account.
### Income tax return and Section CE of form 730
Every frontier worker must file the Italian income tax return (form 730) by the ordinary deadline of May or, in the full version (Redditi PF), by the established deadlines. In Section CE, income from foreign sources (employment income from Ticino) and the foreign tax credit due must be indicated, according to the rules of the IT–CH Double Taxation Convention signed on 9 December 1976. If the Swiss tax is higher than the tax due in Italy, the frontier worker will receive a refund. Consult an accountant specialised in frontier workers or check with the Italian Revenue Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate) for the details of your situation.

### Distances and border crossings From the floor of the Valcuvia valley, the routes towards Canton Ticino essentially converge on the A8 motorway towards the A26 and then on to the Brogeda border crossing, or on the road network leading to Ponte Tresa via Lake Ceresio. For health coverage, any switch from LAMal to the Italian system or vice versa must be managed at the start of the employment relationship.

## Key facts - What: New border agreement between Italy and Switzerland - When: Signed on 23 December 2020, effective from 1 January 2024 - Where: Canton of Ticino and Italian border regions - Who: Ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023 - Amount: Old frontier workers exemption up to €7,500; new frontier workers exemption of €10,000 - **What**: Double Taxation Convention - When: Signed on 9 December 1976 - Where: Italy and Switzerland - Who: Tax administrations of the two States - Amount: Tax credit in the EC framework of 730 to avoid double taxation
Moving to Verbania to work in Canton Ticino is a choice that affects hundreds of Italian workers every year. The Piedmontese city, overlooking Lake Maggiore, is located a short distance from the main crossings to Ticino, but the geographical proximity does not tell the whole story: the real journey times, the availability of public transport and, above all, the taxation that applies to the income of employees in Switzerland count.
### The Tax Framework: Tax at Source and New Deal The basic principle remains ## Practical analysis
Evaluating Verbania as a residential base means comparing at least four dimensions: connections, cost of living, operational taxation, and employment prospects. None of these dimensions is secondary: a cheaper apartment in Verbania can be offset by high transport costs, or by an unfavorable exchange rate.
### How much Swiss contributions weigh on the salary The withholding tax on the Swiss salary is not the only item: the worker also pays Swiss social contributions. AHV/IV/EO requires 5.3% borne by the employee, ALV/ALC 1.1% (with a cap of CHF 148,200), LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector, and LPP between 7% and 18% by age bracket, starting from age 25. On the Italian side, IRPEF remains structured in brackets: 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% above €50,000. The combination of these elements determines the net pay.
### The EUR/CHF exchange rate as a daily variable The salary is paid in Swiss francs, but the daily expenses of a resident in Verbania are mostly in euros. The exchange rate therefore affects real purchasing power: in recent years the franc has remained historically strong against the euro, with phases of significant appreciation. For those who receive their salary in CHF and spend in EUR, it is worth monitoring the exchange rate and evaluating advantageous conversion tools, such as the [CHF/EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange).
### Often underestimated recurring costs The cost of living in Ticino is on average higher than in Italy, but those residing in Verbania avoid daily Swiss expenses (groceries, dining, private healthcare). However, significant items remain: cross-border transport (fuel, tolls, possible vignette), health insurance under LAMal — which for Permit G holders provides the right to choose between the Swiss and Italian system, with adult deductibles between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500 — and the annual [tax return](nav:tax-return) in Italy. For a structured comparison between the two realities, the [cost of living Ticino vs Italy](nav:cost-of-living) tool is useful.
### Who manages what: agencies to know Federal and cantonal tax rates are established by laws and administered by the AFC/ESTV at the federal level and by the cantonal tax administrations. Statistics on cross-border workers are instead collected by USTAT for Canton Ticino, while on the Italian side INPS, the Revenue Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate) and MEF operate. It is important not to confuse roles: the FSIO manages social insurance (AHV/IV), not tax rates, and the FSO is the federal statistical office. ## What to do before moving
### Step 1 — Verify your tax status Before signing any rental contract in Verbania, you need to clarify whether you fall under the "old" or "new" cross-border worker rules. Your status depends on the date you started working in Switzerland relative to 17 July 2023. This distinction determines whether you qualify for the €7,500 exemption or the €10,000 allowance, with direct effects on the [net salary calculation](nav:calculator).
### Step 2 — Obtain the G Permit The G Permit is the specific residence title for cross-border workers, issued by the competent cantonal authorities. For Italian citizens the procedure is simplified thanks to the Agreement on Free Movement, but it is essential to submit the required documentation and meet the employment requirements.
### Step 3 — Registration and social coverage Once the permit is obtained, the Swiss employer registers the worker with the AVS/AI/IPG, unemployment insurance (AD), and, where applicable, the LPP (occupational pension) schemes. On the Italian side, registration with INPS remains necessary for the recognition of contribution periods and the future pension. For health coverage, the LAMal applies: G permit cross-border workers have the right to choose between Swiss and Italian health insurance. The choice should be weighed by comparing premiums, coverage, and claims handling, also with the help of the [LAMal and insurance tool](nav:health).
### Step 4 — Income tax return in Italy Even though the income is taxed in Switzerland, the cross-border worker is required to file an income tax return in Italy, entering the foreign income and the tax credit in section CE of the 730 form. Failure to file can result in penalties and issues with the Tax Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate).
### Step 5 — Border crossings, traffic and travel times From Verbania, the main border crossings into Ticino can be reached in different times depending on the hour. Planning your routes and knowing the [waiting times at the border crossings](nav:border) is essential to avoid chronic delays. Those who prefer public transport can consult the cross-border transport options and the lines available in Ticino. For a full overview of historical traffic, the page on [border crossing queue history](nav:traffic-history) is also available.
### Practical scenario A worker who moves to Verbania and is hired in Ticino with an indicative mid-range gross annual salary will have to manage: Swiss source tax withholding, AVS/LPP/LAINF contributions, Italian income tax return with tax credit, CHF/EUR exchange for household expenses, and health coverage under LAMal. Careful planning of these items, supported by the tools on the site, helps avoid unpleasant surprises at the end of the year.

item.title: Travelling accident at the border: LAINF coverage
item.description: You are covered by LAINF insurance during the commute between Italy and Switzerland. Practical Guide to Coverage, Complaint Procedures, and Deadlines.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - LAINF covers accidents during the commute from Italy to Switzerland - Direct route covered; detours and alternative routes excluded from coverage - Reporting must take place within the deadlines provided to the insurer by the employer
## Key facts - What: Accident during the usual home-work route - Who: Frontier workers (G permit) employed in Switzerland - Where: Border routes (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa) and Ticino road - Coverage: LAINF – Accident Insurance Law (0.7–1.5% contribution) - Protection: Medical expenses, hospital expenses, compensation for incapacity for work, pension in case of disability
Working in Switzerland as [frontaliere con permesso G](nav:permits) means being automatically covered by LAINF (Accident Insurance Act) insurance. It is not a choice: it is mandatory by Swiss federal law. Your employer pays the contribution (0.7–1.5%) and you are enrolled. An accident that occurs while commuting from home (in Italy) to the workplace (in Switzerland) is covered by this coverage.
LAINF stands for the Swiss Federal Accident Insurance Act. It is mandatory for all employees in Switzerland, including border workers with a G permit. It is not optional: the employer has a legal duty to register its employees. The insurer (usually SUVA, but may be another designated entity) provides coverage for accidents on the The daily reality of a cross-border worker (frontaliero) is a continuous commute: you leave home, cross the border (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa), reach your company, and return. Throughout this entire journey, you are 'under protection' under LAINF. But what does this mean in practice?
Imagine working at a Ticino-based company (for example, in Mendrisio, Lugano, or Bellinzona). Every morning you cover the same route: perhaps 30–50 km from your home to the border and then on to the company. This is your 'usual commute'. If one day a car hits you at the Chiasso border crossing and you are injured, the LAINF insurer pays for everything: ambulance, hospitalization, medical care. If you cannot work for 2 months because of the accident, you receive an indemnity (usually a percentage of your salary) for that period. If the accident leaves permanent scars or reduces your working capacity, you receive a pension. You do not have to pay anything out of your pocket for these benefits.
This works because your employer has paid the LAINF contribution (between 0.7% and 1.5% of your annual salary) to a specific insurer (often SUVA, but also other entities designated by the employer). That contribution covers accident risks. For the cross-border worker, this is doubly important: workplace risks plus the risks of the cross-border commute.
### Standard commute vs. business trip: what changes
Here an important distinction comes into play. LAINF covers the 'usual' home-to-work commute. But what happens if your employer sends you on a business trip to another city (for example, a meeting at another office in Switzerland, or a company event)? Or if your boss asks you to deliver goods to a client?
If you are on a business trip (meaning your employer has tasked you with going somewhere other than your usual office), you are still covered by LAINF. However, the coverage is different: it is no longer 'in itinere' (home-to-work commute), but a 'professional' accident (arising from your work activity). Practically speaking, you are covered in the same way, but the administrative category is different. If you are injured while on a business trip for work, LAINF still pays.
Check your [contributions on your payslip](nav:payslip) to make sure your employer has correctly paid the LAINF contribution. The problem arises if you decide to make a voluntary deviation. Imagine: you should go directly to the company, but you decide to stop by a friend's place for breakfast. Or you decide to take a completely different route out of curiosity. In that case, if you are injured during the deviation, there may be a reduction in coverage or an exclusion (depending on how significant the deviation is and the insurer's assessment).
### Cross-border workers and border crossings: a specific risk situation
The cross-border worker who crosses the Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, or Ponte Tresa checkpoints daily has a slightly higher risk exposure than a Swiss worker who reaches the company 5 km away. Cross-border traffic is heavy, especially during peak hours (morning 7–9 am, evening 5–7 pm). Queues at the border crossings are frequent and can cause stress, rushing, and risky behaviors (sudden lane changes, excessive speed, distraction).
Under Swiss LAINF law, there is no special 'subcategory' for cross-border workers facing additional risks. You are covered in the same way: if an accident occurs during the commute, it is a commuting accident (in itinere) and LAINF steps in. Your entitlement is identical to that of any other employee in Switzerland.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). If you are injured during your commute to and from work, act quickly. The procedure is simple, but timing matters.
### First step: assess the situation and seek medical help
If the injury is serious (car accident, major trauma), call 112 (or the local Swiss emergency number 144 for an ambulance). Do not move the body if there are significant injuries. If the injury is minor (small fall, light bruising), you can go directly to the emergency room or to your general practitioner.
### Second step: gather evidence and details
If you were in a car accident, make sure a police report is filed. Take photos of the scene, collect the details of any witnesses (names, phone numbers). Note the date, time, exact location, and what happened. If you received medical care, keep all documents: medical reports, prescriptions, medical certificates.
### Third step: notify your employer
Inform your employer of the injury as soon as possible. The law does not set a specific deadline, but best practice is to notify them within the same day or the following day. The employer is required to report the injury to the LAINF insurer (usually SUVA or another body) within a certain period set by the insurance contract and Swiss law.
### Fourth step: fill in the claim form
The LAINF insurer (through the employer) will provide an official claim form. This form requires: date and time of the injury, exact location, detailed circumstances, any witnesses, description of the injuries, and treatment received. Complete the form carefully and attach the medical documentation.
### Fifth step: follow the benefits process
Once the claim has been submitted, the insurer examines the case. If it is recognized as a commuting accident (in itinere) covered by LAINF, the insurer begins to cover the medical costs. If you remain in hospital, the insurer coordinates directly with the hospital facility in Ticino or in the canton where you are receiving care. Days of incapacity are compensated starting from the first day (or sometimes from the third, depending on the policy). If you remain unable to work for a long time, you can check your [unemployment rights and benefits](nav:unemployment).
### Important timelines and deadlines
There is no rigid nationwide 'deadline schedule' for reporting a commuting accident. However, there is a strong recommendation to act within a few days. If you wait weeks, it may become difficult to gather evidence, witnesses may no longer remember the details, and doctors may not link later treatment back to the original injury.
If the insurer denies coverage (for example, claiming that it was not a regular commute or that there was a voluntary deviation), you have the right to file an appeal. Appeal deadlines are governed by Swiss legislation and depend on the canton. It is advisable to consult a legal advisor specialized in Swiss labor law if the appeal is complex.
### Where to turn and what you need
For tax and contribution matters, your employer deals with SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) or the relevant cantonal bodies. For the specific LAINF insurance, responsibility lies with the chosen insurer (often SUVA). If you reside in Italy and work in Switzerland (G permit), the Italian INPS does not intervene on Swiss accidents: it is the exclusive competence of Switzerland.
Practical tip: Before you find yourself in this situation, ask your employer which LAINF insurer is assigned to your company and how to contact them in case of injury. Having the phone number at hand (perhaps saved in your phone) can make a difference when you need to act quickly.
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to check that your LAINF contributions have been paid correctly.

The Italian income tax return must be filed by 30 September (form 730) or 30 November (form Redditi PF). Registration with LAMal must be completed within three months of starting work. The G permit must be renewed periodically, generally every five years or when changing employer.

### Frequently asked questions
How long does it take to reach Lugano from Campione d'Italia? By car, the journey takes about 20-30 minutes, depending on traffic. By boat, the time rises to 40-50 minutes, but the route offers a panoramic view of Lake Lugano.

New cross-border commuters benefit from a €10,000 allowance; income exceeding this is taxable in Italy.
Is withholding tax also deducted in Italy? No. Withholding tax is deducted exclusively in Switzerland by the employer. Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit indicated in section CE of the 730 (or in section CE/CR of the Redditi PF form).

item.title: Border worker over 55, job change in Switzerland: what to know
item.description: Relocating after 55 years as a border worker: impact on Permit G, second pillar, tax at source and new rates 2024-2033.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 (signature 23/12/2020) - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500, transitional regime 2024–2033 - New frontier workers: deductible €10,000, tax at source only in Switzerland - compulsory LPP from 25th year of age, with contribution bands 7–18%
## Key facts - **What**: Changing employer or canton after the age of 55 as a border worker - When: Transitional regime 2024–2033 for old border workers - Where: Canton Ticino (and in the alternative Graubünden, Valais) - Who: Border employee with G Leave - Amount: Exemption €7,500 (old) or deductible €10,000 (new) - Reference: New Agreement signed 23/12/2020, ratified Law 83/2023 - Double taxation: Italy-Switzerland Convention of 9 December 1976
The New Border Agreement, signed on 23 December 2020 and in force from 1 January 2024, redesigns the tax rules for those who work in Canton Ticino and reside in Italy. Italian ratification came with Law 83 of 13 June 2023. For a worker over 55 who evaluates a relocation, the first distinction to be made is between old border worker (hired before 17 July 2023) and new border worker. The category determines whether it benefits from the exemption of €7,500 with the transitional regime 2024–2033 or from the exemption of €10,000.
### Who is considered border and what changes for the tax The income tax at source is withheld exclusively Changing jobs after the age of 55 brings with it questions that touch three fronts: tax, social security and insurance. At the tax level, the mechanism of the tax at source does not change: Switzerland withholds the tax and Italy recognizes a tax credit to avoid double taxation. On the other hand, the difference between the old and new frontier is played on the extent of the exemption and the duration of the transitional regime. For workers who were already frontier workers before 17 July 2023, the exemption of €7,500 applies with a gradual decrease until 2033; for new frontier workers, the most generous deductible of €10,000 is valid, without decalage.
### Impact on second pillar and pension LPP (occupational pension) is compulsory from the age of 25 for employees subject to the AVS, with an insured minimum wage and contribution rates ranging from 7% to 18% according to age group. Changing employer does not lose the accumulated old-age credit: the LPP account in the fund of the previous employer remains active, or it can be transferred to the pension fund of the new employer (redemption or transfer). For a person over 55, the decision to change employment a few years after retirement must also be evaluated in the light of the exit strategy and the possible early withdrawal of the LPP capital.
### Scenario: what happens when you change jobs A worker considering a relocation to Ticino might wonder if the new employer applies
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Before signing a new employment contract, it is helpful to follow an orderly path. The first step is to determine whether you are an old or new cross-border worker, because your tax treatment depends on this. The second is to verify that the new job falls within the conditions of the G Permit and, in case of a change of canton, which additional requirements apply.
### Step-by-step procedure 1. Status check: old cross-border worker (before 17/7/2023) or new cross-border worker. From 1 January 2024, with the ratification of Law 83/2023, the new regime is fully applied. 2. Payslip control: source tax must be withheld in Switzerland, at the rates set by the AFC/ESTV at the federal level and by the cantonal administrations. The Italian IRPEF rates (23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% above €50,000) only matter for calculating the tax credit in the CE section of the 730 form. 3. LPP check: the new employer is required to join a recognised pension fund; check the contribution bracket and coordinated salary. 4. Notification to INPS: any update of the insurance position for the Italian pension, with a possible request for the totalisation of contributions. 5. LAMal choice: confirmation or change of the right of option for health insurance.
### Useful tools and next steps To simulate the tax effect of a job change, the [cross-border salary calculator](nav:calculator) is available, which allows you to compare source tax withholding between the old and new regime. For those considering a transfer of the LPP account or a voluntary buy-back, the [pension and retirement](nav:pension) section collects dedicated guides on LPP and AVS. item.title: Switzerland: Income and savings at all-time highs in 2025
item.description: In 2025, adjusted disposable income per capita exceeds CHF 65,124 (+36% real on 1995) and voluntary savings reach 19.3%.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Adjusted disposable income per capita 2025: CHF 65,124 - Voluntary savings at 19.3% of adjusted gross disposable income - Total savings at 27.4% of adjusted gross disposable income - Real growth in purchasing power: +36% compared to 1995
## Key facts - **What**: Adjusted disposable income per inhabitant and savings rate at all-time highs - When: Data 2025, published today Tuesday by the UST - Where: Switzerland (aggregated national data) - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Amount 1: CHF 65,124 of adjusted disposable income per capita (2025) - Amount 2:40,083 francs in 1995 (comparison basis) - Amount 3: 27.4% overall savings rate (2025) vs 19.6% (1995) - Amount 4: 19.3% voluntary savings (2025) vs 9.7% (1995)
Swiss families have never been so financially sound. This is certified by the data released today, Tuesday, by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), published at the same time as the 2025 national accounts with updated data on Gross Domestic Product. In 2025, the adjusted disposable income per inhabitant reached CHF 65,124, the highest level in the entire historical series. Net of inflation, this corresponds to a real growth of almost 36% compared to 1995, when the figure stopped at 40,083 francs. The average purchasing power of the Swiss is therefore much higher today than it was a generation ago.
### Saving: always a share ## A national average that weighs differently on the standard of living The picture drawn by the UST is an overall photograph: he photographs Switzerland as a whole, with the adjusted disposable income per inhabitant exceeding 65,000francs for the first time and the voluntary savings rate reaching 19%. But the same methodological note of the Federal Statistical Office draws attention to what the average hides: the increase in the cost of housing, health insurance premiums and other compulsory expenses continues to weigh asymmetrically on many families, especially on low- and middle-income households.
For those who live and work in Canton Ticino, these national data should be read with a specific lens. The border canton has for years had a structurally higher cost of living — in particular for rents, sick pay premiums and consumer goods — than the reference Italian regional averages. An average Swiss purchasing power in real growth of 36% compared to 1995 does not automatically translate into greater spending or provisioning capacity for Ticino's domestic economies, which are confronted with peculiar housing and health dynamics. For border workers with a G permit, who return daily to Italy, the issue is even more complex: gross income is expressed in Swiss francs, but a significant part of consumption — mortgage or rent, food expenditure, supplementary health — is supported
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## What to do: read the data without being misled by the average The publication of the 2025 national accounts by the FSO provides a useful opportunity to review your personal financial situation, without taking it for granted that the national average corresponds to your own.
### Operational checklist for cross-border workers and residents - **Check your real net income**: recalculate your actual pay slip in euros using the current exchange rate, because purchasing power depends on the CHF/EUR ratio and not only on the nominal amount in francs. The [CHF/EUR exchange rate comparator](nav:exchange) allows a quick check. - Fixed cost pressure: LAMal premiums, rent or mortgage instalments, cross-border commuting costs (fuel, motorway vignette, parking, any public transport) are the items that weigh most on your savings capacity. A simulation with the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) helps you understand how much you actually keep in your pocket. - Pension planning: assess whether contributing to pillar 3a still makes tax sense, even under a cross-border regime with a G permit. The contribution threshold and benefits depend on your pension position and your link with AHV/LPP. - Goal-based saving: build an emergency fund in euros — not only in francs — to avoid having to reconvert currency at unfavourable times. The FSO snapshot shows that Swiss households set aside more, but says nothing about the currency composition of savings.
### Three things not to do 1. Take it for granted that the national figure applies to your own household economy: the FSO states this explicitly. 2. Ignore the impact of the increase in health insurance premiums on your savings capacity: in Canton Ticino, the average premium is historically among the highest in Switzerland. 3. Plan your savings only in francs: for a cross-border worker who spends in euros, a share held in euros reduces currency risk.
### Next steps The FSO published the data today as part of the 2025 national accounts: no linked administrative deadlines are indicated for citizens. The most useful time to act remains the next tax return, when you can assess the effectiveness of the savings and pension choices made during the year. For those who want to start from a concrete simulation of their net salary, the reference tool on the site is the [net salary calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator).
*Source: [rsi.ch](https://www.rsi.ch/info/economia/Gli-svizzeri-non-hanno-mai-guadagnato-e-risparmiato-come-oggi--4010966.html)*

item.title: Wages and contracts: the CGIL Ticino proposal for employment
item.description: CGIL Ticino Olona denounces inflation and decline in manufacturing. Proposes a law on procurement to protect wages in Legnanese.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - CGIL Ticino Olona denounces inflation and decline in manufacturing in Alto Milanese - In Q1 2026, 30% of companies recorded a decrease in turnover - Trade union proposal: law to protect wages in procurement and subcontracting - Gasoline over 2 euros per liter, wages have not kept pace
- **Who**: Mario Principe, Secretary General of CGIL Ticino Olona - What: Proposed law on procurement and collection of signatures for wage protections - Where: Alto Milanese, Legnanese, CGIL Ticino Olona territory - When: Resumption of activity after summer break 2026 - Legnanese economy: 4 billion of declared income, 59% of employees - Manufacturing decline Q1 2026: 30% companies with decreasing turnover - Investments: programming shares dropped from 62% to 49%
As activities resume after the summer, CGIL Ticino Olona turns the spotlight on the economic crisis affecting the families of Alto Milanese. Secretary General Mario Principe launches a clear warning: the pressure of inflation, the increase in fuel and energy costs are likely to turn into a permanent erosion of wages and purchasing power. But the problem is not isolated to the price at the pump.
Petrol over two euros per litre represents the visible symbol of a deeper difficulty. Behind there are international tensions that affect energy markets, but also Italian structural issues: energy dependence, energy policy choices, ### The issue of transparency along the supply chain
CGIL Ticino Olona's proposal is based on a simple but fundamental principle: those who work at the same site and carry out the same activity cannot be treated as a series B worker just because their employment relationship goes through a contract. For this reason, CGIL calls for the application of truly representative collective agreements and economic and regulatory conditions consistent with the work actually carried out.
However, the problem goes beyond individual conditions. The longer and more opaque the subcontracting chain becomes, the more difficult it becomes to know who is really responsible for working conditions and safety. Responsibility tends to dissolve along the supply chain, with each link in the chain unloading on the other the burden of ensuring decent standards. CGIL Ticino Olona claims clear responsibility along the entire supply chain, so that it is not possible to hide behind organisational complexity.
According to CGIL Ticino Olona, it is necessary to definitively stop the practice of the maximum reduction as a mode of competition when wages, rights and safety are compressed. A company must be able to compete because it is more efficient, more innovative and more skilled, not because it pays workers less.
This is not a proposal against companies, but against a model of competition that puts correct companies and incorrect companies on the same
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What does CGIL Ticino Olona ask for in its bill proposal
CGIL Ticino Olona has launched a bill proposal accompanied by a signature collection campaign. The objective is twofold: first, to ensure that workers in outsourced and subcontracted services are subject to the same representative collective agreements and the same economic and regulatory conditions as direct workers of the contracting entity; second, to clearly trace responsibility along the entire supply chain, so that it is not possible to place on subcontractors the burden of ensuring workplace safety and dignity.
The proposal addresses a question that concerns the economic model of the territory itself. It is not simply a sectoral trade union claim, but rather a reflection on the quality of development in the Upper Milanese region and Ticino, where modern economy must be based on skilled labor, recognized competencies and dignified wages, not on a spiral of job precariousness.
CGIL Ticino Olona also asks the political establishment to discuss the proposal substantively, not merely to sign it. It is about addressing a question that concerns the economic model of the Country and the quality of development in the cross-border territory. The signature collection campaign represents a mobilization signal, but the true paradigm shift requires regulatory intervention and collective awareness.
The dynamics of the labor market in border territories is integrated. Pressures on wages and working conditions do not stop at the border. Problems of precariousness in Italian outsourced services can influence wage expectations even in Switzerland, and conversely, some of the workers operating in Ticino live just a few kilometers from the Legnanese region. When the cost of living increases simultaneously on both sides of the border, it becomes even more critical that wages are protected and revalued, not compressed.
CGIL Ticino Olona poses an essential question: if the cost of living continues to grow, do we want to continue reducing the value of work or do we finally want to build an economy in which those who work can live with dignity from their own work? This question deserves an answer from the political establishment, businesses and civil society.
For those who wish to better understand wage dynamics and the comparison between the Swiss labor market and the neighboring Italian one, [a calculator is available to simulate net salary](nav:calculator). This tool can help visualize differences in economic treatment and the weight of inflation on incomes from a cross-border perspective.

item.title: Statute S and 13th AVS: Ticino asks for more funds
item.description: Canton Ticino claims federal co-financing for 1,700 Ukrainian refugees and 13th AVS. Cantonal government vs Bern: impact on taxes and the labour market.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Ticino requests that Bern covers the costs of the S status for 1,700 Ukrainian refugees - The 13th AVS requires about 15 million additional financing from the Canton - Only 25% of Ukrainian refugees in Ticino have found work; competition with "border jobs" is an obstacle
## Key facts - **What**: Claim of federal co-financing by statute S (transformation into permit B after 5 years) and 13th AVS - When: Today's meeting of the cantonal government and deputation of Ticino - Where: Canton Ticino (1,700 Ukrainian refugees) - Who: Marina Carobbio Guscetti, Bruno Storni, Cantonal Government - Amount: ~30 million from January per ordinance; ~15 million additional AVS costs - Barrier: 25% employment among refugees; competition with frontier workers on the labour market
The Canton of Ticino does not intend to take on the new federal burdens on its own. At today's meeting, the cantonal government and the Ticino deputy to the Federal Chambers launched a call in Bern: the Confederation must participate in the costs of the S statute for Ukrainian refugees and in the financing of the 13th AVS. Marina Carobbio Guscetti, President of the Council of State, was clear: "Given the financial results of the Confederation, I think there is a margin to do so".
### Statute S and permit B
Bern has decided to extend the S statute for those who come from Ukraine and have served in the military. In addition, after 5 years, it will be transformed into ### How the 13th AVS affects border crossers
The 13th AVS is nothing new for pensioners in Switzerland. However, the way it is financed — and who pays the bill — directly touches the cantonal budgets. If you reside in Ticino and receive AVS benefits (as a border worker who has paid contributions in Switzerland), the 13th is already paid. The problem, from the cantonal point of view, is that Bern wants to offset the cost by supplementing its income with the additional taxes of the cantons.
This dynamic has an indirect implication on the cantonal services you use on a daily basis: if Ticino loses 15 million in revenue to the Confederation, it will have to downsize elsewhere — reducing investments in infrastructure, health, education, or raising taxes. For the border worker resident in Ticino, it means monitoring tax developments. If the Canton compensates for the loss with increases in cantonal or municipal taxes, your tax burden may increase. ### The Ticino labour market under pressure
The employment situation of Ukrainian refugees (25% employment in Ticino) reveals a broader dynamic: the Ticino labour market structurally suffers from a shortage of quality jobs. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to Monitor in the Coming Months
The discussion between the cantonal government and Bern will focus on three crucial decisions. The first concerns the determination of federal co-financing for the S status: Bern will decide whether to participate in the costs of maintaining the 1,700 refugees and their labor and social integration. A negative answer would mean that Ticino would have to find alternative resources — by increasing cantonal or municipal taxes or cutting public services.
The second decision is on the financing method for the 13th AVS. Although the benefit is already active for AVS beneficiaries, the methods of cantonal coverage could change. If Ticino is forced to cede the additional revenue to Bern, it could increase ordinary cantonal tax to compensate.
The third concerns flood funding. If you live in affected areas (including Vallemaggia), delays in federal funds could slow down reconstructions, infrastructure restoration, and support for damaged businesses. Keep an eye on announcements from the Ticino Region and the individual affected municipalities.

If you receive AVS in Switzerland: Verify through the [AVS calculator](nav:pension) whether the 13th is already included in your annual benefit and what amount you receive. Also monitor communications from the Ticino Cantonal Office of Social Security for any increases in cantonal taxes.
If you are looking for work in Ticino: The debate on 25% employment of refugees raises the question of the quality and quantity of available positions in the Canton. If you are looking for a position, diversify your search profile (continuous training, sectoral switching, specialization) to stand out from the competition for low-skilled roles. Access [Ticino job opportunities](nav:jobs) and evaluate training paths that make you a more attractive profile compared to cross-border competition.
