item.title: AVS-INPS Totalization: How Demand Works
item.description: Total contributions between AVS Switzerland and INPS: requirements, forms and calculation of the pension for border crossers Ticino-Italy.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Totalisation: sum of Swiss and Italian insurance periods - It is used when the minimum contributions in a single country are not reached - Application with separate forms at AVS and INPS - Pension calculated pro-rata for each country
## Key facts - **What**: Procedure for totaling insurance periods between AVS and INPS - When: Upon reaching retirement age (different rules for CH and IT) - Where: Cassa AVS Swiss competent and INPS office of reference - Who: Worker with contribution periods in Switzerland and Italy - How: Separate application to each entity, then pro-rata calculation - Legal basis: EC Regulation 1408/71 (replaced by 883/2004) and bilateral CH-EU agreements on social security - Outcome: Two separate pension treatments, proportionate to the contributions paid
Contribution totalization is the procedure that allows a worker with contributory careers in several countries to add up the insurance periods completed in each of them to access a pension. For a Ticino border worker who has paid AVS contributions in Switzerland and INPS contributions in Italy, the mechanism is decisive: without totalization, short periods in a country risk not generating any income.
### When the totalization is triggered The totalization is activated when the applicant does not reach, with the only contributions paid in a single country, the minimum period required for old-age pension. In Switzerland, the reference is the AVS ### How the pro-rata pension is calculated The pro-rata principle is simple in its formula, less intuitive in the numbers. Each country calculates a theoretical pension as if the insured person had paid all contributions only into its own system, then reduces it in proportion to the contributions actually paid on its territory compared to the totalised amount. As a result, a cross-border worker with long periods in both countries will receive two pensions, while someone who worked mainly in Switzerland will get a higher AVS pension and a small INPS share, and vice versa. For the Italian portion, the prevailing IRPEF rates apply, with brackets of 23%, 35% and 43% depending on overall pension income.
### Which documents to prepare The application requires personal identification documents (ID, Italian fiscal code), employment certificates showing the periods of work in Switzerland and in Italy, and any contribution statements issued by both the AVS fund and INPS. For cross-border workers who have changed status — for example after the entry into force, on 1 January 2024, of the new Agreement signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Law 83 of 13 June 2023 — it is also useful to attach documentation relating to the G permit and the applicable tax regime. Changes in status or employer can in fact affect contribution continuity.
### Timelines and bureaucratic process Processing times vary: the AVS application is handled by the compensation fund and the competent federal office, while INPS starts its investigation after receiving the linking form. To speed things up it is advisable to submit the application several months before the desired retirement date, so as to allow the necessary exchanges between the bodies. Once both decisions are obtained, the cross-border worker will receive the Swiss AVS pension (in Swiss francs, with a possible reporting obligation in Italy) and the INPS pension (in euros, taxed under the double taxation agreement between Italy and Switzerland, signed on 9 December 1976).
### Tax implications for cross-border workers Foreign pensions are taxed under distinct rules: the Swiss AVS pension is taxable in Italy for the recipient who is fiscally resident in Italy, with a credit for taxes paid in Switzerland in order to avoid double taxation; the INPS pension is taxed entirely in Italy. For 'old' cross-border workers, the EUR 7,500 exemption provided by the 2024–2033 transitional regime applies to employment income and not to pension income, which instead follows the ordinary rules. Explore more about the double taxation agreement and the [salary calculation](nav:calculator) to understand the combined effect on pension income.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Step-by-step procedure for the cross-border worker The first step is to request, several months before retirement, the contribution statement both from the Swiss AVS fund and from INPS: these documents certify the insurance periods accrued and form the basis for totalization. The second step is to fill in the AVS pension application form at the compensation fund, attaching identity documents and employment certificates. The third step is to submit the pension application to INPS, also through a patronato (welfare patronato office), indicating the periods of work in Switzerland and explicitly requesting totalization.
### What to do if the periods do not match It may happen that the periods resulting from the two institutions do not coincide perfectly, for example due to overlaps or contributions paid abroad before the G permit. In these cases it is necessary to produce supporting documentation (employment contracts, pay slips, certificates from the Swiss employer). The AVS fund and INPS can take up to several months to verify, during which the application remains suspended. To avoid delays, it is advisable to gather the documentation in advance and keep a copy of all Swiss pay slips.
### Common scenarios among Ticino cross-border workers A cross-border worker with more than twenty years of AVS contributions and few years of INPS contributions will obtain a full AVS pension and a small INPS share, with separate taxation in the two countries. A worker with a more balanced mixed career will instead receive two pensions of comparable amount, both contributing to forming the pension income. Those with contributions only in Switzerland do not need to activate totalization: the AVS application will follow the ordinary procedure, without involving INPS. Learn more about [LPP contributions and the third pillar](nav:pillar3) to build a supplementary pension.
### Useful tools To simulate the effect of totalization on your future pension, it is useful to start from the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator), which allows you to estimate gross and net income during the working phase and plan the transition to the pension. For contributions paid in Switzerland, it is also advisable to check the [LPP and AVS situation](nav:pension) and, in case of opting for pillar 3a, evaluate its impact on the overall pension. The advice to turn to a patronato or a specialist in cross-border pension planning remains valid for more complex situations, especially in the presence of contribution periods in third countries or changes in status between the old and new Agreement.
Calculate the effect of contributions on your pension now with the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: AVS-INPS totalisation for border workers: how it works
item.description: Cumulate the contribution periods between Switzerland and Italy for retirement. 1976 Convention, New Agreement 2024: practical guide, documentation and calculation of annuity.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Totalization allows for the aggregation of contribution periods between Swiss AVS and Italian INPS for pension calculation. - It applies to cross-border commuters with a work history in both countries, according to the Convention of December 9, 1976. - The New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement (effective January 1, 2024) modernizes the coordination regulatory framework.
## Key Facts - **What**: Totalization of contribution periods between AVS (Switzerland) and INPS (Italy) - When: Convention signed December 9, 1976; New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement entered into force January 1, 2024 - Where: Canton Ticino (Switzerland) and border regions (Italy) - Who: Cross-border commuters who have worked in both countries; INPS, FSIO (Federal Social Insurance Office) - Rates: AVS 5.3% for employees; Italian IRPEF 23%–43% depending on income - Legislation: Convention of December 9, 1976; Italian Law no. 83/2023 (ratification of New Agreement)
The totalization of social security contributions between Switzerland and Italy represents one of the most important mechanisms for cross-border commuters who accumulate contribution history in both systems. This institution allows those who have worked for both Swiss and Italian employers to aggregate contribution periods, preventing periods from 'getting lost' when transitioning from one system to another.
For Ticino cross-border commuters, this topic is particularly relevant. Many started their careers in Italy, subsequently moved to Switzerland, or oscillate between the two systems during their working lives. Totalization ensures that contribution periods paid in one country are recognized when calculating pension entitlement and its overall amount.
### The Legal Basis: From the 1976 Convention to the 2024 New Agreement
The regulatory framework governing totalization is based on two essential pillars.
The first is the Convention on Mutual Assistance in Social Security Matters between Switzerland and Italy, signed on December 9, 1976. This international instrument introduced the principle of totalization of contribution periods, allowing workers not to lose rights acquired in one country when moving to the other.
The second pillar is the New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and entered into force on January 1, 2024. In Italy, it was ratified with Law no. 83 of June 13, 2023. This agreement has modernized and completed the totalization regime, also introducing provisions on withholding tax and tax benefits for cross-border commuters with a G permit.
Totalization operates according to the principle of reciprocal social security solidarity: contributions paid in one state are also recognized in the other, for the purpose of determining entitlement and calculating the pension. The contributions themselves are not summed (as they remain distinct in the two systems), but rather the contribution periods — the years and months of payment — are aggregated to establish access to the pension benefit and its overall amount. To estimate the impact of totalization on your future pension, you can consult the [pension calculator](nav:pension). ### How the totalization mechanism works
Totalization is not an automatic operation, but a procedure that requires awareness and action from the worker. Here's how it concretely works.
When a cross-border commuter ceases working and reaches retirement age, they have the right to request recognition of the contributory periods accumulated in both countries. The competent authorities — the FSIO (Federal Social Insurance Office) for Switzerland and INPS for Italy — coordinate through a bilateral administrative procedure. The cross-border commuter who has worked in both Switzerland and Italy must submit a request specifying all contribution periods in both systems. This documentation is crucial: it serves to demonstrate that the worker has effectively paid contributions or has been covered by the respective mandatory insurance schemes.
Once the periods are accumulated, the pension calculation follows a 'pro-rata' formula: each system calculates its pension amount based on the contributions paid in its own territory, but recognizes the totalized periods to determine if the person is entitled to a pension and according to what amount.
### Practical scenario: Ticino cross-border commuter with a mixed history
Consider the generic case of someone with 8 years of INPS contributions in Italy (accumulated before transferring to Switzerland) and subsequently 17 years of OASI contributions in Switzerland. Without totalization, the cross-border commuter might not reach the minimum contribution required by one of the two systems, thus losing pension rights. With totalization, the total 25 years are recognized and combined.
Specifically: INPS calculates its portion of the pension based on the 8 years of Italian contributions, but recognizes the right to a pension considering the combined 25 years. OASI calculates its portion based on the 17 years of Swiss contributions, similarly considering the 25 years for access. The final pension amount results from the sum of two distinct components: the Swiss OASI pension (calculated on 17 years of Swiss contributions, with a 5.3% rate for employees) and the Italian INPS pension (calculated on 8 years of Italian contributions, with IRPEF rates varying from 23% to 43% depending on the income bracket).
Each system applies its own calculation rules, its own rates, and its own revaluations of contributions over time. The cross-border commuter therefore receives two distinct pension payments: one from Switzerland and one from Italy. Totalization does not merge the two systems but coordinates the recognition of periods, avoiding gaps in the calculation of the benefit. Consult the [tax return](nav:tax-return) to better understand how a mixed contribution history also affects the taxation of future pensions.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### How to apply for aggregation: procedure and documentation
The application process is a delicate stage requiring coordination between the two social security systems. There is no fixed deadline to start the application, but it is advisable to act in advance to avoid delays.
**Required documentation**
The cross-border worker must collect a series of documents that demonstrate the continuity and completeness of their contribution history:
- INPS contribution statements (available from the INPS online portal) - OASI-DI-IC (AVS-AI-IPG) contribution statements from Switzerland (available from the registers of the insured at cantonal offices or directly from the FSIO) - Employment certificates for any missing periods or documentary gaps - Identification documents (passport, identity card) - Certificate of residence
These documents are the foundation of the application: they allow authorities to verify that the worker has indeed paid contributions in both countries.
Where to submit the application
In Switzerland, cross-border workers residing in Canton Ticino can contact the cantonal OASI/DI office (Social Solidarity and Social Security Division of the Ticino DFE) or the FSIO in Bern directly. In Italy, the request for recognition of aggregation must be submitted to INPS, preferably via the online portal or at the competent local office of the place of residence.
The procedure is not linear: the time required for recognition depends on the number and type of periods accumulated, any career interruptions, and the type of insurance (compulsory, voluntary, provisional).
Approximate timelines
Once the complete documentation has been submitted, the recognition of aggregation can take from 3 to 9 months, depending on the efficiency of the relevant offices and the administrative coordination between the two countries. It is not possible to give a precise deadline, as it depends on factors such as the availability of historical documents and any need for clarification or additional information from the worker.
Practical advice is to contact the relevant offices (FSIO and INPS) at least 12–18 months before the expected retirement age, to start the procedure in time and resolve any documentary gaps before the pension begins.
To get an idea of the approximate pension amounts you might receive from Switzerland, use the [pension annuity calculator](nav:pension): it allows you to estimate your OASI (AVS) benefit based on accumulated contributions, facilitating financial planning for retirement.

item.title: Rental vs ownership: the choice of frontiersmen
item.description: Border crossing to Ticino: comparison between owned cars and long-term rental. Analysis of costs, benefits and how to choose the best solution.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Frontiersmen travel high distances daily towards Ticino - Cars with high mileage deteriorate faster and lose value - Long-term rental offers programmable expenses and maintenance included
## Key facts - **What**: Choice between car ownership and long-term rentals for border workers - When: Growing trend in 2026 - Where: Province of Varese towards Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano (Canton of Ticino) - Who: Italian frontier workers - Mileage: Tens of km per route × 5 days/week = thousands of km/month - Solution: Rental with periodic fee (maintenance, insurance, assistance)
Every morning, workers from the province of Varese reach companies, professional offices and health facilities in the Canton of Ticino. Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano: for each of them, the route varies depending on the municipality of residence, the workplace and the chosen pass (see the [tempi di attesa ai valichi](nav:border)), but the car remains an indispensable tool to ensure the continuity of travel.
Driving many kilometres is the norm for the border crossing. What seems like a manageable distance on a weekly basis turns into thousands of kilometers per month when multiplied by five working days and added to family commutes and weekends. The car is not only the means of transport from the crossing to the office: it is the vehicle that supports a mobility with high intensity of use.
### The Impact of Mileage ### When the car no longer suits
Hidden car ownership costs often go unnoticed at the time of purchase. A frontier worker who calculates the cost of mobility frequently makes the mistake of considering only the loan installment, forgetting that the actual price of the vehicle includes advance, interest, insurance, ordinary and extraordinary maintenance, tires, coupons and the residual value of the vehicle at the time of sale. Adding these elements gives a very different picture from the one imagined in the purchase phase.
In addition to numbers, there is also practical management. Taking charge of a car means coordinating a constant series of obligations: finding the most convenient workshops, comparing quotes, monitoring the wear of components, planning coupons with work commitments. An unexpected failure can turn into a serious organizational problem: if the vehicle is stuck in the workshop, those who have to reach the workplace every day are faced with delays, possible absences, and the need to quickly find an alternative means with unexpected additional costs.
For the border worker, ensuring the continuity of movements is not an optional choice: it is a necessity that guides the choice of means of transport. Sometimes, those considering alternatives might consider [i mezzi pubblici disponibili in Ticino](nav:transport), but for the most part having a reliable and predictable car remains central.
## # Long-term rental as
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to Choose the Right Solution
Before deciding between ownership and leasing, the cross-border worker must ask themselves some concrete questions. How many kilometers do you actually drive in a year? What would be the total cost of ownership (purchase, payments, insurance, maintenance, tires, depreciation)? How much would leasing cost with similar parameters? Only by comparing these elements is it possible to make an informed decision.
Ownership remains cost-effective if annual mileage is low and the vehicle is maintained regularly. For those who drive tens of kilometers daily toward the border, the situation changes quickly. A car used intensively accumulates more frequent extraordinary maintenance, loses value more rapidly, and requires constant management that absorbs time and energy, both precious in a cross-border commuting routine.
Long-term leasing offers a simple proposition: predictable expenses in a single payment, ordinary and extraordinary maintenance included, insurance and roadside assistance covered, tire management entrusted to the leasing company, no responsibility for final depreciation. This simplicity represents tangible value for those already managing complex mobility.
### Tools to Evaluate Costs
For the cross-border worker who wishes to compare the two options, the first step is to calculate the total cost of mobility with a privately owned car. This includes not only the financing payment, but every expense item: insurance, preventive maintenance, tire wear, scheduled service, and the value the car will have at the time of sale.
In parallel, it is useful to obtain quotes from long-term leasing companies, specifically for cars suitable for commuting (reliable engine, efficient consumption, comfort and safety). Comparing the total cost of ownership with the total cost of leasing will provide concrete data to guide your choice.
Many cross-border workers will discover that leasing offers not only financial savings, but also freedom from practical management and worry about unexpected breakdowns. In a context where time is precious and the car is a work tool, this simplification has real value. To evaluate in detail the transportation and mobility costs in your specific case, [consult our car cost calculator for cross-border workers](nav:car-cost). Start with your real numbers to make the best decision.

item.title: Entry documents Switzerland: border guides 2026
item.description: Passport, G permit, identity card: mandatory documents and procedures to cross the border. New 2024 Agreement, Ticino crossings, customs controls and tax rebates.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024: taxation changes for those working in Switzerland - Compulsory documents: Italian passport or identity card, G permit (residence), customs checks - Old frontier workers (pre 17/7/2023): exemption €7,500 per year; new frontier workers: €10,000 deductible
## Key facts - **What**: Entry procedure into Switzerland and documentation for Italy-Switzerland border workers - When: In force from 1 January 2024 (New Frontier Agreement) - Where: Ticino crossings (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa) and SECO/SEM offices - Who: G-permit frontier workers, employees and the self-employed - Permit: G Permit for residence in Italy + work in Switzerland; B Permit for residence in Switzerland - Primary document: Valid passport or Italian identity card with 3 months residual validity - Regulatory deadline: Law 83 of 13 June 2023 (Italian ratification of the New Agreement)
On 1 January 2024, the New Frontier Agreement amended the rules on taxation, permits and entry into Switzerland for those working across borders. To regularly cross the crossings (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo and others), the border worker must have specific documents and comply with precise procedures: it is not a secondary formality, but an essential requirement to legally work and support the contributory and tax obligations towards the Swiss AVS and the Italian INPS. Switzerland, although not an EU member, requires strict documentation ### How the New 2024 Agreement Rules Taxation and Entry
The border crossing into Switzerland does not only face customs controls: its tax status is governed by the Italian-Swiss Convention (signed on 9 December 1976) and the New Frontier Agreement (signed on 23 December 2020, in force from 1 January 2024). Switzerland applies tax at source (Swiss tax withholding) directly on the paycheck, while Italy avoids double taxation by granting a tax credit in [quadro CE della dichiarazione 730](nav:tax-return). This means that the border worker pays taxes in Switzerland (not in both countries), and Italy recognises what has already been paid north of the border. The procedure is coordinated: the Swiss employer pays the tax at the source, the border worker declares in Italy, the Revenue Agency accredits the refund.
Daily entry to the crossings does not require a specific customs declaration for income only: customs checks physical goods (cars, goods, contraband, money over €10,000) and not the compensation already received. However, the registration of the G permit with the Italian municipality of residence is a formal prerequisite that Swiss customs can verify in the event of a random check. A border crossing without a registered G permit is not legal and risks administrative sanctions, revocation of the permit itself and blocking of future renewal. SECO and SEM operate in synergy: registration deficiencies are tracked and communicated between offices.
### Set to
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step Procedure: How to Obtain a G Permit and Cross the Border
Step 1: Registration with Your Italian Municipality of Residence Before starting work in Switzerland, the cross-border worker must go to their municipality of residence (Lugano, Bellinzona, Mendrisio, Locarno, Chiasso, etc.) in the Canton Ticino and formally notify the intention to work across the border. The municipality issues a residence certificate with mention of cross-border work and communicates personal data to SECO (Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs). This step is preliminary: without municipal registration, the G permit application cannot proceed.
Step 2: Request for G Permit from Local Swiss Authorities The Swiss employer or the cross-border worker themselves requests the G permit from the SEM office (State Secretariat for Migration) of the canton where work will take place (Ticino, Valais, etc.). The permit is granted after verification of the availability of jobs for cross-border workers (annual quota set by SECO) and the economic situation of the company. SECO sets a maximum quota of cross-border workers hired each year: if the quota is exhausted, the application can be rejected even if the company is solid. This is one of Switzerland's main controls on new entries.
Step 3: Registration with the Swiss Municipality of Work (Optional but Recommended) Not mandatory, but many Swiss municipalities register cross-border workers for statistical and administrative purposes (USTAT collects data). It does not create residency in Switzerland and does not involve additional local social obligations.
Step 4: First Entry and Crossing the Border Once in possession of a G permit, passport/identity card, the cross-border worker can cross the border posts (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa, etc.). Swiss customs conduct random checks; a thorough check requires presentation of the G permit, Swiss income tax return (by end of February each year), and any goods subject to customs declaration. An identity card or passport is always mandatory. Customs also check alignment between the registered permit and data from the Italian municipality of residence.
📊 **Document Checklist at the Border**: - Italian passport or identity card (valid with at least 3 months remaining validity) - G permit (paper or digital depending on the canton) - Tax return 730 (not mandatory at the border, but recommended to demonstrate fiscal compliance) - Residence certificate from the Italian municipality (optional, to support the permit)
### Deadlines and Renewals: What to Do Each Year
The G permit has limited validity (generally 1-5 years depending on the canton) and requires renewal before expiration. Deadlines vary by canton (Ticino, Valais, Graubünden). Renewal must be requested well in advance (at least 2-3 months before expiration), otherwise the cross-border worker loses legal status as a cross-border worker and risks more severe checks at border posts, up to being blocked from entering Switzerland.
The [tax return with model 730](nav:tax-return) must be submitted by April 30 each year to the Italian Revenue Agency. This document is essential to recover the Swiss tax credit and demonstrate bilateral fiscal compliance. Those who do not submit the 730 do not access the refund and face double taxation.
To verify social security rights (AVS, LPP) and contributions paid, the cross-border worker can consult the [refund and pension calculator](nav:pension) provided by Frontaliere Ticino and check the account statements provided by SECO. Additionally, the [G vs B permit comparator](nav:permits) helps choose the most convenient status over time.
⚠️ Warning: Failure to file the 730 tax return does not invalidate the G permit, but compromises tax recovery and may raise suspicion in case of more severe customs checks. Consult promptly the [Swiss net salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the impact of the exemption on your paycheck.
### What Changes in 2026: New Bilateral Agreement Fully in Force
In 2026, the New Bilateral Agreement for Cross-Border Workers is fully in effect (no longer in transition phase). This means the distinction between old cross-border workers (€7,500 exemption) and new cross-border workers (€10,000 exemption) remains stable until at least 2033. The entry procedure DOES NOT change: documents, G permit, border posts, customs checks remain identical. However, tax planning must account for the permanent exemption and the absence of further exemption increases. Those in the transitional regime until 2033 benefit from a gradual progression toward the ordinary tax rate and are protected by safeguard clauses.

- **What**: Renovation with reduction in personnel and materials - When: Announced 26 August 2026, implementation 2026-2027 - Where: Raiffeisen Switzerland (208 banks, 748 branches, St. Gallen) - Who: Raiffeisen Swiss Cooperative - Savings amount: CHF 60 million, up to 180 seats affected - Half-year profit: CHF 659 million (+18.9% year-on-year) - Operating revenue: CHF 2.04 billion (+7.6%) - Assets under management: CHF 289.8 billion (+2.7%)
Raiffeisen Switzerland announced a significant restructuring on 26 August 2026: cuts of up to 180 jobs out of 10,972 full-time equivalents, with the aim of saving around CHF 60 million in personnel and material costs in the coming months.

Operating revenues increased by 7.6% to CHF 2.04 billion, while operating costs grew by 3% to CHF 1.16 billion: a ratio that testifies to the institute's efficiency.
The bank benefited from substantial liquidity inflows. In the semester, new funds came in for 3.3 The restructuring of Raiffeisen fits into a broader context of rationalisation in Swiss financial services. The announced cuts — up to 180 posts — represent about 1.6% of the group's workforce (180 out of 10,972). Although the official source does not specify the geographical locations of the cuts, the implications for the Swiss labour market are relevant. Raiffeisen is one of the country's leading financial institutions, with a strong presence in numerous cantons, including Canton Ticino where it operates with its own subsidiaries.
For those working in the banking or financial sector in Switzerland — including frontier workers employed at Swiss institutions — announcements of this type indicate a structural trend towards automation and operational efficiency. The bank pointed out that more than half of the cuts will take place through “natural” means (turnover, retirements, reduction of external staff), which suggests that not all posts will be eliminated through direct redundancies. This is a relevant element for current employees: most of the changes will happen without drastic actions.
### The Financial Stability Perspective
Paradoxically, the cuts are announced at a time of strong economic growth. The increase in net profit of 18.9%, revenues of 7.6% and the raising of new funds of 3.3 billion suggest that the restructuring is not dictated by financial difficulties, but by strategies
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). Those working at Raiffeisen or other Swiss banks can monitor developments through official channels of the institution. The bank is organized as a cooperative and details of restructurings are communicated through official press releases and shareholder assemblies.
For cross-border workers employed in Switzerland and receiving salaries in Swiss francs, occupational changes at major banks like Raiffeisen have indirect impacts: they influence regional economic stability, career opportunities, and potentially sector salary levels.
### Tools to assess your situation
If you are an employee of Raiffeisen or another Swiss bank:
1. Review your contract and legal protections: in Switzerland, dismissals for economic reasons follow precise procedures defined by the Code of Obligations, which guarantees minimum notice periods and, in case of redundancy, possible compensation.
2. Consult the Human Resources staff at your branch to understand if the restructuring might affect your specific role or sector.
3. If you are a cross-border worker and receive a salary in CHF, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate various salary scenarios and understand the fiscal and contributory impact.

### Opportunities in the market
Paradoxically, cuts at major banks can generate opportunities elsewhere. For those who are cross-border workers and seeking or changing jobs in Switzerland, it is useful to monitor [job opening announcements](nav:jobs) at Swiss companies that could benefit from turnover in the banking sector.

item.title: Frontier 2026: taxation, new agreement and exemption
item.description: From 2024, the new Italy-Switzerland agreement reduces taxes for border workers: €7,500 exemption for the old, €10,000 for the new. Here's how it works.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- New tax agreement effective from January 1st, 2024: tax allowance and tax credit for cross-border workers - Tax allowance €7,500 for existing cross-border workers (before 17/7/2023), €10,000 for new ones - Source tax withheld only in Switzerland, tax credit recovered in Italy in section CE of the 730 return
## Key facts
- **What**: New Italy-Switzerland agreement on cross-border worker taxation with tax allowance and tax credit - When: Effective from January 1st, 2024 (Italian ratification: Law 83 of June 13, 2023) - Where: Ticino Canton and Italian cross-border province (Permit G) - Who: Cross-border workers with dependent employment income in Switzerland - Tax allowance: €7,500 annual for existing cross-border workers, €10,000 annual for new cross-border workers - Source tax: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7–1.5% - Tax credit: Recovery in section CE of the Italian 730 tax return - Base convention: December 9, 1976 (double taxation)
The new Italy-Switzerland cross-border worker tax agreement, signed on December 23, 2020 and effective from January 1st, 2024, represents a significant reduction in the tax burden for those working in Ticino and residing in Italy. The Italian ratification, which occurred with Law 83 of June 13, 2023, consolidated the new rules on tax allowance, source tax, and tax credit. The Convention to avoid double taxation between the two countries, signed on December 9, 1976, remains the regulatory foundation, but the more recent agreement introduces more favorable mechanisms for cross-border workers.
### Tax allowance for existing and new cross-border workers
For cross-border workers already holding status before July 17, 2023, the tax allowance is €7,500 per year, applied under transitional regime until December 31, 2033. For new cross-border workers (from July 17, 2023 onwards), the tax allowance increases to €10,000 per year, with no specified time limit. This amount represents the non-taxable income in Switzerland in calculating source tax and is considered in section CE of the Italian tax declaration for the tax credit.
### How source tax and tax credit work
Source tax on employment income is withheld exclusively by Switzerland. The Swiss employer automatically remits tax based on mandatory contributions: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% charged to the employee, plus AD/AC at 1.1% (with cap CHF 148,200), LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5%. Italy, based on the Convention to avoid double taxation, does not apply additional withholding on the same income base. The cross-border worker recovers the excess tax burden through the tax credit in section CE of the [tax return](nav:tax-return) Italian (730). If Swiss taxes exceed Italian tax (IRPEF), they receive a refund; if they are insufficient, they pay a balance adjustment. ### Old cross-border worker scenario
A cross-border worker already in service benefits from an annual exemption of €7,500. The gross income earned in Switzerland is reduced by the exemption in the calculation of Swiss withholding tax. In Italy, the same income is subject to IRPEF according to progressive tax rates: 23% up to €28,000, 35% up to €50,000, 43% above €50,000. Without the tax credit, the cross-border worker would face double taxation on both sides (both Swiss and Italian). Thanks to the agreement, they recover through Schedule CE of the Italian tax return the Swiss taxes already paid, reducing the total tax burden and often obtaining significant refunds.
### New cross-border worker scenario
A cross-border worker who started employment from 17 July 2023 onwards is entitled to an annual exemption of €10,000, €2,500 more than for old cross-border workers. This higher exemption reduces the Italian taxable base proportionally. Like the old cross-border worker, they recover the tax credit in the 730 form by reporting the Swiss taxes paid. The advantage of the higher exemption remains unchanged during the 2024–2033 period and beyond, with no time limitations communicated so far.
### Differences between old and new cross-border workers
The difference of €2,500 between the two exemptions (€7,500 vs €10,000) is not merely an administrative detail: it represents a reduction in the Italian taxable base calculable on average IRPEF rates (approximately 30–35%). For old cross-border workers, the transitional regime expires on 31 December 2033. After that date, the regulation could be subject to modifications, currently not specified in new communicated agreements. New cross-border workers, on the other hand, benefit from the €10,000 exemption without duration limits declared so far, offering greater regulatory stability.
### Mandatory Swiss contributions and LAMal
In addition to withholding tax, the cross-border worker pays contributions [AVS/AI/IPG](nav:pension) at 5.3% of income, AD/AC at 1.1% (on income up to CHF 148,200), LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5%. The second pillar (LPP) varies between 7% and 18% depending on age from 25 years onwards. For health insurance (LAMal), the cross-border worker with Permit G has the right of choice: they can insure themselves in Switzerland with adult deductibles between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500, or in Italy. This choice impacts the total tax burden and health coverage. ### Come compilare il 730 con il credito d'imposta
Il frontaliere deve compilare la dichiarazione dei redditi italiana (730) riportando il reddito lordo estero (quello dichiarato in Svizzera prima della franchigia) nel quadro E. Nel quadro CE, indica il credito d'imposta, che corrisponde alle imposte svizzere effettivamente versate: imposta alla fonte e contributi AVS/AI/IPG (5.3%), più AD/AC (1.1%), LAINF (0.7–1.5%). Non è sufficiente indicare solo la franchigia: è necessario documentare l'intera struttura reddituale e supportare il credito con certificazioni svizzere.
### Documentazione necessaria e scadenze critiche
La documentazione essenziale include: certificato di reddito svizzero (emesso dal datore di lavoro svizzero, simile al CUD italiano), estratto conto contributivo AVS/AI per verificare i contributi versati, dichiarazione svizzera Steuererklärung (facoltativa se le ritenute coprono il debito, ma consigliabile per documentare il credito). Le scadenze sono: il 730 italiano va presentato entro il 30 giugno dell'anno seguente (per il reddito 2025, scadenza 30 giugno 2026); la dichiarazione svizzera, ove obbligatoria, segue i tempi cantonali ticinesi (solitamente marzo–aprile); i ristorni del credito d'imposta italiano arrivano in genere tra 60–120 giorni dopo l'elaborazione dell'Agenzia delle Entrate.
### Strumenti di calcolo e supporto pratico
Per stimare il carico fiscale effettivo con la franchigia applicata e il credito d'imposta recuperato, è essenziale utilizzare uno strumento di simulazione. La piattaforma di Frontaliere Ticino mette a disposizione un [calcolatore](nav:calculator) che consente di inserire il reddito lordo svizzero, la categoria di frontaliere (vecchio/nuovo), i contributi obbligatori svizzeri (AVS, AD, LAINF, LPP) e genera una stima netta della busta paga e del debito/credito fiscale italiano. Per domande sulla procedura, è possibile rivolgersi all'Agenzia delle Entrate (sportelli nelle province di Como, Varese, Lecco) o ai CAF convenzionati. In Svizzera, il cantone Ticino (DFE – Dipartimento Finanze ed Economia) e l'Amministrazione Federale delle Contribuzioni (AFC) forniscono supporto su contributi e dichiarazioni svizzere. Uno strumento complementare è il [comparatore di permessi](nav:permit-compare) per verificare se il Permesso G rimane la scelta ottimale rispetto al Permesso B di residenza.

item.description: Health rights for border workers Ticino-Italy: LAMal and INPS in comparison, reimbursement procedures and how to choose the most convenient insurance.

## In a nutshell - LAMal: Swiss health insurance with option right for border workers G - 2020 Agreement: CH-IT health coordination from 1 January 2024 - LAMal Deductible: CHF 300-2500 per year for adults - Italian INPS: manages refunds for those residing in Italy
## Key facts - **What**: Right of option for border workers with Permit G on the insurance choice - When: Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 (signed 23 December 2020) - Where: Canton of Ticino and neighbouring Italian provinces (CH-IT coordination) - Who: Frontier workers with G Permit; INPS, BAG/UFSP, LAMal insurers - Coverage: LAMal: deductible CHF 300-2500 adults; copayment 10% - Regulations: Double taxation agreement 9 December 1976; Frontier Agreement 2020
The Ticino-Italy border health system operates according to a principle of coordination between Switzerland and Italy, enshrined in the New Frontier Agreement that entered into force on 1 January 2024. Those who work in Switzerland with a G Permit and reside in Italy have the right of option: they can choose to cover themselves with LAMal (Swiss health insurance) or maintain the coverage of the Italian INPS system.
This choice has direct implications on the reimbursement of healthcare expenses. LAMal is the main insurer in Switzerland, with deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 for adults, plus a 10% co-payment up to a maximum. The expenses covered depend on the contract chosen and the services provided in the territory For the border worker, the choice between LAMal and INPS is not trivial. LAMal offers direct access to Swiss doctors and hospitals, generally quick advice and short waiting lists. However, out-of-pocket costs (deductible and copayments) can be significant: CHF 300-2500 deductible per year, plus 10% copayment up to a maximum. For those with high healthcare needs, the calculation of total costs requires attention.
On the contrary, those who choose to remain in the Italian INPS system benefit from a wide coverage of basic medicine, with hospitalizations and surgeries normally borne by the public service. However, Italian public border hospitals often have longer waiting lists. Accessing Swiss services as an INPS insured requires a coordination procedure and is not always immediate. [Verificare il costo della vita nei due Paesi](nav:cost-of-living) can help you estimate the economic weight of your insurance choice.
### Coordination between Switzerland and Italy The Double Taxation Convention (signed 9 December 1976) and the 2020 Frontier Agreement provide that the country of primary insurance is responsible for reimbursements. If you are LAMal insured and undergo a hospital visit in Como (Italy), your claim should normally be forwarded to your LAMal insurer, who will assess whether to recognise the benefit according to Swiss criteria.
Conversely: if you are an INPS member and visit a hospital in Ticino, INPS may request a pre-authorization or a
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). The choice between LAMal and INPS must be made at the time of issuing Permit G. It is not a decision you can postpone: the responsible insurer is designated from the beginning, and changing it requires formal procedures with the competent authority.
First step: ask for information from the competent office. If you are a new cross-border worker with Permit G, contact: - SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) Switzerland: provides information on insurance schemes and LAMal options - Visa office of your Italian province: clarifies whether INPS coordination is already established in your case - Tax Agency / local INPS: if you choose the Italian system, register and ask for a complete overview of your rights
Second step: choose the insurer (if LAMal). If you opt for LAMal, contact directly an accredited Swiss insurance company operating in Ticino. Compare contracts, deductibles, co-payments. Explicitly ask which services are covered in Italy (not all insurers cover them in the same way). Also verify if the insurer has simplified reimbursement agreements with hospitals or border Italian doctors.
**Third step: keep complete documentation.** For each medical visit, hospitalization or prescribed medication, ask for a detailed receipt, written diagnosis (if available) and signed medical prescription. These documents are essential for requesting future reimbursements. Keep them for at least 5-7 years, also in digital format (photos/scans).
Fourth step: request reimbursements promptly. Do not wait months: send your reimbursement request within the timeframe established by your insurance (usually 30-90 days from the date of care). Attach all original documents or certified copies. If you receive an initial denial, ask in writing for the reason and consider filing an appeal.

item.title: Ticino and Bern: the crucial issue of refreshments
item.description: On 27 August in Bellinzona, discussion on the suspension of refreshments and negotiation with the Confederation and the Lombardy Region
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The Council of State of Ticino met today with the Deputation to the Chambers for the autumn session of the Swiss Parliament (14 September-2 October) - Central theme: precautionary suspension of refreshments and dialogue with the Confederation and the Lombardy Region - The Deputation, chaired by Bruno Storni, received delegations on tourism and security policy
## Key facts - **What**: Meeting of the Ticino State Council and the Ticino Deputation to discuss cantonal concerns in view of the parliamentary session - When: 27 August 2026; parliamentary session from 14 September to 2 October - Where: Bellinzona (main meeting); Gordola (celebrations for the President of the Deputation) - Who: Council of State of the Canton of Ticino; Ticino Deputation to the Federal Chambers (chaired by National Councillor Bruno Storni) - Border issue: Cautionary suspension of refreshments; ongoing dialogue with the Confederation and the Lombardy Region - Deadline: End of year for navigation concessions on the lakes of Lugano and Maggiore
### Bellinzona, the traditional meeting precedes the autumn session
The Ticino State Council met today with Ticino representatives in the Federal Parliament — the usual preparatory meeting for the autumn session that will start on 14 September and end on 2 October. At the center of the political confrontation, the recurrent theme of the increasing transfer of burdens from the Confederation to the Cantons and the impact ### The refreshment mechanism and its meaning for border workers
Refreshments represent one of the fundamental mechanisms that link the Swiss tax system to the Italian border municipalities and directly affect the daily reality of the Ticino border worker. For those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy, understanding the dynamics of refunds means understanding how income taxation is redistributed between the Swiss authorities and the Italian municipalities of the provinces of Varese, Como and Brescia.
Refunds constitute the portion of the tax at source that Switzerland pays to the Italian municipalities of residence of border workers according to the bilateral agreements between the two States. When this transmission is cautiously suspended — as occurred and discussed in today's meeting in Bellinzona — the financial flow to the beneficiary Italian municipalities is temporarily interrupted. This interruption has a direct impact on municipal finances and, consequently, on the local public services that border workers resident in Italy use daily: from road maintenance to public transport services, from educational services to local welfare.
The Ticino Deputation emphasized the precautionary suspension during today's meeting because it represents an element of administrative instability that affects both the Italian host communities and the well-being of the border workers themselves. Suspension is not a final decision,
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How cross-border workers can monitor the evolution of the issue
For the cross-border worker who resides in Italy and works in Switzerland, monitoring the evolution of the issue regarding remittances means staying informed about official communications from the Swiss Confederation, the Ticino Parliamentary Delegation, and the Lombardy Region. During the autumn session of the Swiss Parliament — which starts on September 14 and concludes on October 2 — the Ticino Parliamentary Delegation will presumably bring updates on this bilateral negotiation. The mayors of border municipalities (Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano, Varese, Como) are often the first to disseminate news on negotiation outcomes, as they are directly interested in maintaining remittances in their budgets.
A useful information channel is the following: the official website of the Ticino Parliamentary Delegation will publish reports from the autumn session in which this issue will be discussed. Furthermore, press releases from the Lombardy Region and the interested mayors will be disseminated through Italian local media (Como and Varese provinces) and Swiss media (Ticino media). The cross-border worker can subscribe to the mailing lists of their municipalities of residence in Italy to receive official updates on this matter.
### Impact on the payslip and income tax return of the cross-border worker
The suspension of remittances does not directly impact the [payslip of the cross-border worker](nav:payslip) from an immediate quantitative perspective: the Swiss source tax continues to be applied according to the current federal, cantonal (Ticino), and municipal rates. However, the correct functioning of double taxation Italy-Switzerland and the Italian tax credit remains linked to the regular transfer of data between Swiss administrations and the Italian Tax Authority.
If the suspension of remittances reflects broader administrative misalignments between the two states, the cross-border worker may experience delays in completing their income tax return (section CE of form 730) or in collecting the tax credit owed. It is therefore advisable to regularly verify the status of your tax communications through [the tax calculator dedicated to cross-border workers](nav:calculator), simulating the impact of your taxation according to the current source tax rates and comparing the amount withheld in Switzerland with the credit due in Italy.
It is also appropriate for the cross-border worker to communicate with their Swiss employer to verify that they are correctly applying source tax according to federal legislation and Ticino cantonal legislation, without variations caused by the administrative suspension of remittances (which concerns exclusively the transfer of funds between states, not the calculation of the withholding from payslip).
### Future developments and monitoring of the resolution
During the autumn session, the Ticino Parliamentary Delegation will meet with Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis and, for the first time, the new General Director of the Postal Service, Pascal Grieder. These meetings could bring clarification on the timing of the resolution of the precautionary suspension and on coordination between the various administrative levels. Cross-border workers can stay updated through official communications from the Ticino Parliamentary Delegation, available on the official website of the Swiss Parliament, and through bulletins from Italian mayors.
Given the strategic importance of the year-end deadline, it is essential to monitor developments in the coming weeks. If the suspension were to continue beyond this deadline, the cross-border worker could decide to contact their Italian municipality of residence to report the situation and receive information on any expected delays in managing remittances and related public services.
For a more complete understanding of how the remittance system connects to personal taxation and Italy-Switzerland fiscal agreements, [consult the dedicated guide on remittances](nav:ristorni) available on our site. Stay informed on every development of the Swiss Confederation-Lombardy Region negotiation, especially given the year-end deadline for resolving the issue and the impact that a positive resolution will have on the administrative and financial stability of your communities of residence in Italy.

item.title: Swiss healthcare expenses reimbursable in Italy for border workers
item.description: What health expenses incurred in Switzerland are reimbursable in Italy for border workers, with the necessary procedures, limits and documents.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Swiss health expenses can be deducted in Italy with the EC framework of 730 - Tax credit avoids double taxation on income from work - Frontier workers with G permit have the right of option LAMal - The Italian IRPEF starts from 23% up to 28,000 euros
## Key facts - **What**: Health expenses incurred in Switzerland reimbursable or deductible in Italy - When: Annual income tax return with CE framework - Where: Canton of Ticino and border Italy - Who: Border workers with G permit, Revenue Agency, INPS - Amount: Adult LAMal deductibles from CHF 300 to 2,500 - Rate: IRPEF 23% up to 28,000 euros, 35% from 28,001 to 50,000, 43% over 50,000 - Agreement: New tax agreement in force from 1 January 2024
The management of health expenses for those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy is a node that touches thousands of border workers in the Canton of Ticino every year. The starting point is the Double Taxation Convention between Italy and Switzerland, signed on 9 December 1976. This convention stipulates that income tax at source is only withheld in Switzerland. Italy avoids double taxation by recognizing a tax credit, which is recovered by filling out the EC framework of the model 730.
For border workers with a G permit, the Swiss health insurance LAMal provides for the right of option. This means that the worker can choose whether to maintain Swiss coverage or join the health system ## Practical implications for the border crossing
Those who reside in Italy and work in Ticino must understand how to deal with healthcare expenses incurred in Switzerland. The general rule is that documented medical expenses can be deducted in the Italian tax return, using the EC framework for the tax credit. The mechanism works like this: Swiss employee income is declared in Italy, Italian tax is calculated, and the credit is subtracted for taxes already paid at source in Switzerland.
Reimbursable or deductible health expenses include medical services, drugs, hospitalizations and other items provided for by Italian legislation. The critical point is the documentation: you need the Swiss receipt or invoice, possibly with the indication of the service and the amount in francs. The conversion into euros must be done at the average exchange rate of the tax period, a step that requires attention because the CHF/EUR rate can also vary significantly during the year.
### Comparison between old and new frontier workers
The difference between old and new frontier workers also affects health expenses. The old frontier workers, with an exemption of 7,500 euros and transitional regime until 2033, have a reduced tax base in Italy. The new frontier workers, with a deductible of 10,000 euros, start from a different situation. In both cases, the deductible health expenses are added to the other deductions provided for by the Italian system, but ## Operational procedure for reimbursement
The path to obtaining reimbursement or deduction of Swiss healthcare expenses in Italy consists of precise steps. The first step is to gather all documentation: invoices, receipts, payment confirmations issued by Swiss healthcare facilities, doctors, or pharmacies. Each document must indicate the service, date, amount in francs, and details of the person who incurred the expense.
The second step is conversion to euros. Italian regulations require the use of the average exchange rate for the tax period. It is advisable to check the applicable exchange rate and keep track of the method used, so it can be justified in case of an audit by the Italian Revenue Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate).
### Completing Form 730
The third step is completing section CE of Form 730. In this section, income earned in Switzerland is declared and the tax credit for taxes withheld at source is calculated. Healthcare expenses must be indicated in the section dedicated to deductible charges. The amount in euros, converted as described, must be reported using the codes provided for healthcare expenses.
The fourth step is verifying limits. Deductible healthcare expenses are subject to a deductible, as provided by Italian regulations. Not all expenses are fully deductible: some items have specific maximum limits. It is advisable to check the documentation before submission to avoid errors that could trigger audits or requests for additional information.

To best manage these steps, the Frontaliere Ticino tax calculator allows you to simulate the impact of healthcare expenses on your tax return and estimate the tax credit. The [salary calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to check the net salary received in Switzerland and compare it with the Italian net salary.
The deadline for submitting Form 730 is the ordinary one provided by the Italian tax calendar. Those with income from Swiss employment must also pay attention to declaration obligations related to the tax credit. Documentation must be kept for the period required by regulations in case of assessments.
To delve deeper into your tax situation, compare scenarios, and prepare documentation, use the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) and consult the guide on [tax returns](nav:tax-return). item.title: Withdrawal according to the LPP border pillar: rules, taxes and strategy
item.description: When the LPP can be withdrawn, how taxation works in Switzerland and Italy, and what exit strategy suits the Ticino border crossing.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The LPP withdrawal is only possible in strict cases: first home purchase, independent activity, final exit Switzerland - Taxation at source in Switzerland varies by canton; in Italy IRPEF applies with tax credit - The new border agreement 2024 changes the deductible: €10,000 for new border crossers, €7,500 for old border crossers - Double taxation is avoided through the 1976 convention and the EC framework of 730
## Key facts - **What**: Early or final withdrawal of the second LPP pillar for Italy-Switzerland border workers - When: On the occurrence of qualifying events (home, independence, expatriation, retirement) - Where: Canton of Ticino (Chiasso, Brogeda, Gaggiolo passes) and all of Switzerland - Who: Frontier workers with G permit, LPP pension fund, Revenue Agency, AFC/ESTV - Amount: LPP rates 7–18% by age group from the 25th year; tax at source CH + IT income tax - Regulations: Convention 9/12/1976, New Agreement 23/12/2020 (effective 1/1/2024), Law 83/2023
The withdrawal of the second LPP pillar represents one of the most important financial decisions for the border worker working in Canton Ticino. The Swiss law on occupational pensions (LPP) provides that the capital accumulated in the pension fund can only be withdrawn in strictly defined circumstances: purchase of the first home of residence, start of an independent gainful activity, permanent exit from Switzerland or reaching the age of ### Taxation in Switzerland: tax at source on capital When the frontier worker requests the withdrawal of the LPP capital, the pension fund applies the tax at source on the capital (Kapitalauszugssteuer). This is a separate tax from the income tax at source and follows its own rates, generally progressive by tiers of capital withdrawn. In the Canton of Ticino, as in the other cantons, the rate depends on the gross amount of the levy and the civil situation (single, married, with children). The tax is withheld at source from the pension fund and paid to the cantonal administration of contributions. There is no withholding "in both countries" on capital: Switzerland taxes at source, Italy taxes on declaration with the tax credit mechanism to avoid double taxation.
### Taxation in Italy: personal income tax and tax credit In Italy, the LPP capital withdrawn contributes to forming the total income of the border worker and is subject to personal income tax according to the ordinary steps: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000. However, the Double Taxation Convention of 9 December 1976 (art. 18) confers on Switzerland the right to tax pension capital disbursed from Swiss coffers. Italy avoids double taxation by granting a tax credit equal to the Swiss tax paid, to be calculated in the EC framework of the 730 or PF Income form. The credit cannot exceed personal income tax (IRPEF)
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Step-by-step procedure for withdrawal 1. Check with your LPP pension fund which withdrawal case applies (home purchase, independence, permanent departure, retirement). 2. Request the official withdrawal form and a simulation of the Swiss withholding tax (gross amount, estimated tax, net payout). 3. For home purchase: prepare the preliminary notarial deed or final deed, cost estimates, and any mortgage commitment. 4. For permanent departure: obtain confirmation of the cancellation of the G permit from the Cantonal Migration Office (SEM/cantonal authority) and proof of new Italian residence (civil status certificate). 5. Receive the net bank transfer to your bank account (preferably a cross-border CH or IT account with a SEPA IBAN). 7. ### Deadlines and key documents The withdrawal application must be submitted before the qualifying event (e.g., before the final deed for a home purchase, before the cancellation of the G permit for permanent departure). The pension fund's processing times vary (usually 4–8 weeks). For the Italian tax return, the capital must be declared in the year of receipt (cash basis principle). Keep: signed withdrawal form, receipt for Swiss withholding tax (pension fund certificate), received bank transfer, and the Italian tax return with box CE completed.

item.title: Diesel: 17 cents off until Wednesday, August 26th
item.description: The Italian government extends the 17% discount on diesel excise duties until Wednesday 26 August. Average price: diesel €2.20/litre, petrol €2.08/litre.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Discount on diesel extended until Wednesday, August 26, 2026 - Reduction of 17 cents per litre between excise duties and VAT - Average diesel price €2.20/litre, petrol €2.08/litre - Funds terminated, no new extension planned
## Key facts - **What**: Extension of the discount on diesel excise duties - When: Until Wednesday 26 August 2026 - Where: Italy - Who: Ministries of Economy and Environment (Giorgetti and Pichetto Fratin) - Amount: 17 cents per litre (excise + VAT) - Original deadline: Monday, August 24, 2026 - Start of measurement: 28 July 2026
The Italian government extended the discount on diesel fuel until Wednesday 26 August, granting a short extension of only two days compared to the original deadline of Monday 24 August. The measure, formalized through a decree signed by the Minister of Economy Giancarlo Giorgetti and the Minister of the Environment Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, maintains an overall reduction of 17 cents per liter resulting from the excise duty cut and the consequent effect on VAT applied to the final price of fuel.
With the subsidy still active, the average price of diesel is around 2.20 euros per litre. For petrol, on the other hand, there is no intervention, and the average indicated remains around 2.08 euros per litre. This differential between the two fuels is due exclusively to the government measure on diesel: without the discount, the price would rise significantly.
### Chronicle ## What it means for those heading to Switzerland
Cross-border workers who work in Switzerland and reside in Lombardy, Piedmont, or the Ticino border areas face daily cross‑border mobility expenses. The car is the main means of crossing the Chiasso, Brogeda and Gaggiolo border points — not only for freight transport, but above all for daily commuters who, from Varese, Como, Busto Arsizio and neighbouring towns, reach the cantons of Ticino and inland Switzerland.
Fuel prices directly affect the monthly budget of these workers. With the discount of 17 cents per litre still active until Wednesday, 26 August, those who refuel in Italy save a non‑negligible amount. A commuter who uses 40 litres per month saves today about €6.80 per month compared with the price without the discount. For those who consume 60 litres per month (longer journeys or additional routes), the discount represents a saving of about €10.20 per month. On the mobility‑cost calculator you can estimate your personal saving.
### After 26 August: return to full prices
Once the extension ends, the price of Italian diesel will rise significantly. Without the 17‑cent reduction, those who refuel in Italy will have to face higher prices, with the increase having an impact proportional to the amount of fuel consumed for commuting. Cross‑border workers who have planned their refuelling knowing the deadline should start monitoring prices in the last weeks of August, possibly anticipating refills before the measure ends.
It is important to stress that gasoline is excluded from this concession, so drivers of petrol‑powered cars have not benefited from the discount. This creates an asymmetry: diesel‑car owners have enjoyed an economic advantage, while others have not.
### The role of mobile excise duties and price volatility
The mobile excise‑duty system, although useful in the short term, does not provide long‑term price stability. As described earlier, the financing of the discount depends on VAT revenues during periods of rising global prices. When prices fall or stabilise, VAT receipts drop, reducing the funds available for cutting excise duties. This is exactly what has happened: the international tensions and geopolitical factors that had fuelled the initial rise have partly eased, and the accumulated funds have been exhausted.
For cross‑border workers, this means they cannot rely on permanent fuel discounts. Find out in the [report on the cost of living Ticino‑Lombardia](nav:cost-of-living) how fuel fits into overall commuting expenses.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to organize supplies: practical actions
There are a few days left before the expiry of the measure. If you are a frontier worker who crosses the Brogeda or Chiasso crossings on a daily basis and consumes Italian fuel, you can take some concrete actions to reduce the impact of the price increase that will come after August 26.
### Step 1: Track the price until Wednesday, August 26
Many fuel distributors in Italy (both local and large chains) publish their prices online and through dedicated apps. In the next 24-48 hours, check where the cheapest gas stations are located on your way to Switzerland, between Varese and the border. It is not uncommon to find differences of a few cents between different stations, even in the same area. Anticipating your supply by a few days could save you a few euros.
### Step 2: Calculate your monthly consumption and plan
If you don't know the average monthly consumption of your car, now is the time to calculate it. Formula: litres supplied divided by kilometres travelled = average consumption per litre. Once you have this figure, you'll know exactly how much you'll save until August 26th and how much more you'll spend after that. For example, if you consume 50 liters per month, after August 26 you will pay 8.50 euros more than today (50 × 0.17). Multiplied by 12 months, the annual impact is 102 euros. These numbers become even more significant if your consumption is higher.
